item.title: Public transport under attack: the SEV raises its voice against violence
item.description: On 3 September, the SEV union organises a day of action against violence against public transport employees, with events at different train stations.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Day of Action against violence against public transport employees on 3 September. - Increase in verbal and physical aggression from the pandemic. - SEV calls for greater respect and safety.
## Key Facts - **What**: Day of action against violence against public transport employees. - When: September 3rd. - Where: Locarno SBB station, Bern, Lucerne, Thun and French-speaking Switzerland. - Who: SEV Transport Staff Union. - Amount: Around ten attacks on SBB per day.
Violence against public transport staff continues to be a worrying reality in Switzerland. Since the pandemic, verbal and physical aggression has increased significantly and remains at high levels. For this reason, the transport staff union SEV is organising a national day of action against violence and to promote greater respect in public transport on 3 September.
The meeting will take place at Locarno SBB station at 10:30 a.m. "For many colleagues in public transport, attacks have become a sad everyday reality. Some have been insulted, others threatened, physically assaulted or spat upon," says SEV vice-president Barbara Keller. "Current data show that the problem has not decreased. The number of attacks against public transport staff remains at an alarmingly high level."
According to police crime statistics, around two incidents in public transport spaces are prosecuted every day. Violence against public transport staff is an offence that can be prosecuted ex officio and must therefore be prosecuted by the authorities. Despite the many incidents, it is difficult to assess the true extent of this due to the lack of comprehensive data at national level. The SEV intends to bring the issue to parliament during the autumn session and is calling for an interpellation to be submitted to the Federal Council. It is also calling for the establishment of a national system for monitoring incidents of violence against public transport staff.
### The current situation
SBB alone reports around ten attacks on its staff every day. SEV Vice-President Barbara Keller emphasises that "every attack is one too many". To stop this trend, all actors must act together. This requires, among other things, sufficient staff, double support and systematic support for employees after attacks.
With this day of action, the SEV aims to draw attention to the problem of violence at various railway stations and call for greater safety and respect for public transport staff. In addition to Locarno, the SEV will also be present in Bern, Lucerne, Thun and French-speaking Switzerland. ## Practical implications
The day of action organised by the SEV aims to raise awareness among the public and the authorities of the seriousness of the problem of violence against public transport staff. SEV vice-president Barbara Keller said that "every aggression is one too many" and that it is necessary to act together to stop this trend.
### Safety and Support Measures
To tackle the problem, concrete measures such as increased staffing, double accompaniment and systematic support for victims of aggression are needed. SEV President Matthias Hartwich stressed the importance of coordinated action between all actors involved to ensure greater safety and respect for public transport staff.
### Monitoring and interpellation
The SEV intends to bring the issue to parliament during the autumn session and is calling for an interpellation to be submitted to the Federal Council. In addition, the union is calling for the establishment of a national system for monitoring incidents of violence against public transport staff. This system would allow for a clearer view of the extent of the problem and more effective measures to be taken to combat it.
### Comparison with the previous situation
Before the pandemic, attacks against public transport staff were already a problem, but the situation has worsened significantly in recent years. The day of action on 3 September is an important step to draw attention to the difficulties that public transport workers face on a daily basis and to promote concrete change.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ## Concrete actions
To address the problem of violence against public transport staff, a number of concrete measures need to be taken. Here are some actions that can be taken:
### Staff augmentation
Sufficient staff are crucial to ensure safety in public transport. Authorities need to invest in training and hiring new employees to cover shifts and ensure a constant presence in stations and on means of transport.
### Double accompaniment
Double accompaniment can be an effective solution to reduce the risk of aggression. Having two people on board the means of transport can deter potential attackers and ensure a faster response in case of an emergency.

Victims of assault need systematic support to deal with the psychological and physical consequences of violent incidents. Authorities must ensure quick and easy access to psychological and medical support services for public transport workers.

The SEV calls for the establishment of a national system for monitoring incidents of violence against public transport staff. This system would allow for a clearer view of the extent of the problem and more effective measures to be taken to combat it. ### Conclusion
The day of action on 3 September is an important step to draw attention to the difficulties that public transport workers face on a daily basis and to promote concrete change. To ensure greater safety and respect for public transport staff, a number of concrete measures must be taken and action taken together. item.description: Swatch wins in London against Samsung: the court orders the giant to pay $11.6 million for counterfeiting digital dials.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief
- Swatch wins lawsuit in London against Samsung: $11.6 million in damages - Samsung copied digital watch faces with logos of 10 Swiss brands - Approximately 160,000 illegal downloads in the UK and EU between 2015 and 2019
## Key Facts
- **What**: Counterfeit digital watch faces on Galaxy App Store - Where: London Court - Who: Swatch Group vs Samsung Electronics - When: Violations from 2015 to 2019 - Amount: $11.6 million (vs. $170 million requested) - Brands: Breguet, Blancpain, Jaquet Droz, Glashütte Original, Omega, Longines, Tissot, Hamilton, Mido, Swatch - Users: Approximately 160,000 downloads
Swatch has won a significant victory in a case judged by a British court against South Korean tech giant Samsung. The London court has sentenced Samsung Electronics to pay $11.6 million to the Swiss watch company for trademark infringement. The ruling comes after years of litigation on a specific issue: the digital counterfeiting of watch faces.
The story concerns applications that can be downloaded from Samsung's Galaxy App Store platform, available between October 2015 and February 2019. These apps offered watch faces that mimicked protected designs from ten brands of the Swatch Group: Breguet, Blancpain, Jaquet Droz, Glashütte Original, Omega, Longines, Tissot, Hamilton, Mido and Swatch itself. The apps were available both for free and for a fee and recorded around 160,000 downloads in the UK and European Union.
### The incredible gap: from $301 to $11.6 million
What is surprising about the ruling is the enormous distance between the negotiating positions. Samsung Electronics, in fact, was initially willing to pay only $301 to the other party as compensation. Swatch Group, on the other hand, had claimed $170 million for the systematic infringement of trademarks. The British court found a middle ground: $11.6 million. Although it is a fraction of the amount requested by Swatch, the ruling represents a substantial recognition of the damage caused by counterfeiting and the massive spread of fraudulent applications in two important markets: the United Kingdom and the EU.
The lawsuit covered a specific period, from 2015 to 2019, during which counterfeit apps circulated on Samsung's platform without permission. The fact that Samsung was willing to offer less than $300 initially suggests that the tech company knowingly underestimated the reputational and economic damage done to the Swatch Group's luxury brands. The $11.6 million award represents a tangible economic achievement for the Swatch Group in the current business environment. The Swiss company, which is listed on the Zurich stock exchange, has recovered in recent years after a difficult period in the watch industry. A favorable ruling on intellectual property helps to strengthen trademark protection in the global market and sends an important signal to competitors about the cost of counterfeiting.
The proliferation of counterfeit apps on app stores is a growing phenomenon in the digital economy. Unlike counterfeiting physical products, which requires manufacturing infrastructure, digital counterfeiting is facilitated by scalability and the difficulty in controlling millions of applications available on the platforms. In Samsung's case, the 160,000 downloads recorded in the UK and EU highlight the scale of the problem: a significant user base that has come into contact with fake versions of Swatch products.
### The precedent in digital markets
The British court's ruling underlines the importance of local jurisdiction in protecting intellectual property rights. The UK and the EU have some of the strictest standards of protection in the world. This factor has presumably favored Swatch's position in legal negotiation. In addition, the court was able to assess the actual damage in terms of users reached, downloads, potential loss of sales, and reputational damage to the brand.
Swatch's victory not only affects Breguet, Blancpain, Omega, Longines, Tissot, Hamilton and Mido — the partner brands of the Swatch Group — but also the entire Swiss watch industry. Luxury watches represent a product category where design, heritage and brand are fundamental elements of commercial value. Counterfeiting, even in digital form, erodes these intangible elements that Swiss manufacturers have developed and invested in over decades.
### Implications for the Swiss watch industry
The decision sets an important legal precedent: international courts are willing to recognize the damage from digital counterfeiting and award proportionate compensation. This can encourage other Swiss luxury manufacturers to legally protect themselves against similar infringements in other channels, from app stores to social networks, from online marketplaces to e-commerce sites. The message is clear: intellectual property is also protected in digital form and infringements have significant economic consequences. If you're a Swiss consumer interested in technology and watches, the London ruling offers an important practical lesson: the reliability of the source from which you download apps. Counterfeit apps that mimicked Swatch, Omega, Longines, and other brands were available on Samsung's Galaxy App Store, an official platform. This means that even app stores run by big tech manufacturers require careful user verification.
### How to recognize counterfeit apps
The first defense is to verify the developer's name. Legitimate apps from Swatch, Omega, and other luxury brands are published directly by the proprietary companies or clearly identifiable authorized partners. If an app offers popular design watch faces but is not published by the official company, it is almost certainly counterfeit.
Second, look at reviews and the total number of downloads. Official apps from established brands have thousands or hundreds of thousands of downloads with a pattern of verified reviews. Counterfeit apps, even if they are mass-downloaded as in the Samsung case, often have a less professional profile.
Finally, consider the price and features. A legitimate watch face from a luxury brand generally costs between $0.99 and $4.99. If you find deals that are too affordable or apps that promise access to premium content without in-app purchases, be wary.
### What to do if you downloaded a counterfeit app
If you were exposed to counterfeit apps from the Galaxy App Store between 2015 and 2019, there's no immediate risk to your device — it wasn't malware. You simply used an unauthorized product that infringed on the Swatch Group's trademark. You can uninstall the app if you want. Samsung removed all unauthorized apps from its platform after the end of the availability period (February 2019), so exposure to the issue is now historic.
For the future, remember to download phone customization apps (such as smartwatch faces) only from official stores and verified brand profiles. Apple App Store, Google Play Store and Samsung Galaxy App Store have improved control systems compared to the years 2015-2019, but it always remains a shared responsibility between the platform and the end user.
If you are interested in the topic of intellectual property — especially in the context of luxury and Swiss technology — you can learn more about how trademark rights work in the global market. The Swatch Group remains one of the world's largest players in the watch industry and represents excellence in Swiss engineering and design globally. item.title: 2025 parties: 24.6 million, -1 million from 2024
item.description: In 2025, Swiss parties declare 24.6 million francs of revenue, a decrease of about one million compared to 2024. The SP leads with 7.9 million francs.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - 24.6 million: total funding declared by the 9 parties in 2025 - Decrease of ~1 million compared to 2024 (they were 25.6 million) - PS leads with 7.9 million, FDP second with 4.8 million
## Key Facts - **What**: Annual Declaration of Funding of Swiss Federal Political Parties - Who: Swiss Federal Audit Office (SFAO) - When: 2025 (data published by the SFAO) - Where: Switzerland (9 of 10 parties in the Federal Assembly) - Total amount: CHF 24.6 million - Change: -1 million compared to 2024 (3.9% decrease)
The Swiss Federal Audit Office (SFAO) has published data on the revenue reported by political parties for 2025. Nine of the ten parties represented in the Federal Assembly recorded total revenues of CHF 24.6 million, around one million less than in the previous year, when total revenues amounted to CHF 25.6 million. The declarations are made on the basis of the rules on the transparency of the financing of Swiss politics.
The Socialist Party (SP) remains the first in terms of fundraising capacity, with revenues of CHF 7.9 million. It is followed by the Radical Liberal Party (FDP) with CHF 4.8 million, the Swiss People's Party (SVP) with CHF 3.8 million and the Centre Party with CHF 2.7 million. These four parties have representatives in the Federal Council, Switzerland's executive chamber.
Among the four government parties, the SP and the FDP recorded a decrease in revenue compared to 2024, by CHF 0.3 million and CHF 1.8 million, respectively. The People's Party and the Centre, on the other hand, recorded an increase in revenue, by CHF 1 million and CHF 0.1 million, respectively.
### The other parties
Among the smaller parties, the Greens declared revenues of 1.8 million francs, while the liberal Greens reached 1.2 million. Revenues of less than one million francs were declared by the Federal Democratic Union (UDF), the Evangelical Party (ENP) and the Mouvement Citoyens Genevois (MCG). The Lega dei Ticinese, the only party among the ten represented in the Federal Assembly, has not yet disclosed its funding for 2025, representing the only gap in the annual transparency landscape. The overall decline of around one million francs compared to 2024 highlights a downward trend in fundraising in the Swiss political landscape. This figure, despite its apparent numerical modesty (a decline of 3.9% year-on-year), reflects deeper dynamics in Swiss politics and the ability of parties to attract resources from private donors and supporters.
### Internal redistribution
Looking at the internal movements between the main government parties, a mixed picture emerges. While the SP and FDP suffered repercussions in 2025 (-0.3 and -1.8 million respectively), the SVP compensated with a growth of 1 million and the Centre maintained stability with a minimal increase of 0.1 million. The largest relative loss belongs to the FDP, which recorded a 27% drop from its 2024 revenue, suggesting a possible rearrangement of the donor base between centre-right forces.
At the same time, the overall decline did not evenly affect all parties. The Greens maintained a substantial collection (1.8 million), while the liberal Greens remain at 1.2 million. This segmentation of the party landscape shows that the volatility of funding is uneven, with some parties maintaining a stable donor base and others suffering from greater variability.
### Transparency and democratic accountability
The annual declarations published by the SFAO are a pillar of Swiss democratic transparency. They allow citizens to understand how the parties finance themselves and, indirectly, what the economic influence of the various stakeholders is in the Swiss political landscape. The fact that one of the ten parties (Lega dei Ticinese) has not yet provided data for 2025 underlines the importance of systematic monitoring of this information and compliance with federal transparency regulations.

Data on party-reported funding is publicly available thanks to transparency regulations on political financing. item.title: Sick pay premiums Freiburg: reduction and subsidies
item.description: Guide to compulsory health insurance premiums in the Canton of Fribourg: deductibles, alternative models and procedure for obtaining premium reductions
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Health insurance LAMal is mandatory in Switzerland and also valid in Fribourg - Available deductibles range from CHF 300 to CHF 2500 for adults - The Canton of Fribourg offers subsidies (premium reduction) for residents with low income - The registration procedure must take place within 3 months of arrival in Switzerland
## Key facts - **What**: Mandatory health insurance with per capita premiums and variable deductibles - Where: Canton of Fribourg (national LAMal system applied at cantonal level) - Who: All residents in Switzerland must obtain coverage - Deadline: Within 3 months of arrival in Switzerland - Deductibles: From CHF 300 to CHF 2500 for adults - Subsidies: Available for those with insufficient income (cantonal criteria)
### The mandatory LAMal system in the Canton of Fribourg
The [LAMal health insurance](nav:health) is mandatory in Switzerland and also valid in Fribourg. It is a private insurance with per capita premiums, not a tax or salary contribution. Anyone who moves to Fribourg or any other Swiss canton must obtain coverage within 3 months of arrival, otherwise they risk administrative penalties. Each insured person pays their own premium, regardless of income or age (except for young adults up to 25 years old, who benefit from flat-rate reductions). Premiums vary depending on the canton of residence, the insurance company chosen, and the insurance model subscribed to (standard, with reduced deductible, HMO models, etc.). In the Canton of Fribourg, like in other cantons, mandatory insurances must cover all residents according to LAMal regulations, without exclusions for pre-existing conditions or health conditions. Health insurance is therefore the cornerstone of Switzerland's national health protection system.
### Deductibles and coverage levels
The deductible is the amount that the insured person pays out of pocket before the insurance begins to reimburse. In Switzerland, deductibles for adults are standardized at the federal level and are available in six levels: CHF 300, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000, and 2500. Those who choose a higher deductible (for example CHF 2500) pay a lower monthly premium; those who choose a low deductible (CHF 300) pay a higher premium. This choice is individual and can be reviewed every year. In the Canton of Fribourg, each resident receives communications from insurance companies with available premiums, allowing them to compare and choose the deductible level that best suits their health profile and budget. In addition to standard deductibles, some insurance models (such as HMO policies or models with mandatory primary care physician) can offer reduced premiums. These models require consulting a primary care physician first before accessing specialists, but allow significant savings on the annual premium. Fribourg canton, like all Swiss cantons, provides subsidies to reduce health insurance premiums for people with low incomes. The subsidies (also called 'premium payment assistance') are determined at the cantonal level according to income, assets, and household composition criteria.
### How premium reduction works in Fribourg
The procedure to obtain the [premium reduction in Canton Fribourg](nav:health) follows the national system: those with insufficient income can apply to the competent cantonal office (generally the social welfare office or equivalent). Criteria vary from canton to canton, but typically include:
- Gross income below a threshold defined by the canton - Limited assets - Household composition (spouse, dependent children)
The amount of the subsidy depends on the gap between the actual premium and the 'payment capacity' calculated by the canton based on income. It is not possible to provide exact amounts without consulting updated data from Canton Fribourg, but the mechanism is transparent: the subsidy partially or fully covers the difference between what the insured person can afford to pay and the actual cost of the premium.
### Deadlines and documentation
Premium reduction applications must usually be submitted by specific deadlines (often coinciding with the year change, in December). Documentation on income (tax return, pay slips, bank statements) and assets must be provided. The decision is notified in writing, and the subsidy is valid for one year, generally requiring renewal every year.
In Canton Fribourg, subsidy management can take place at the cantonal social welfare office. It is advisable to contact the competent office directly to find out the exact forms and deadlines, as these administrative details are subject to annual variations. Subsidies are not automatic: they must be requested every year by submitting updated documentation. Many residents do not know they are entitled to subsidies and continue to pay the full premium; contacting the cantonal welfare office is the first step to verify eligibility. The procedure is generally free and the assessment requires a few weeks.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### Step-by-step procedure for registration
Step 1: Finding out about available premiums
Within 3 months of arriving in Fribourg (or at the beginning of each calendar year if already resident), gather your identification documents and contact the insurance companies operating in the canton to receive their premium proposals. You can do this online through the insurers' websites or directly at their offices. The offers must include the monthly premium for each available deductible level.
Step 2: Choosing the model and deductible
Assess which deductible level (CHF 300–2,500) and which model (standard, HMO, family doctor model) suits your anticipated medical spending profile. A young, healthy adult might opt for a high deductible and basic model; a person with chronic conditions might prefer a low deductible and broader coverage.
**Step 3: Concluding the contract**
Sign the contract with the chosen insurance company. Coverage will take effect on the 1st of the following month (or from the date you specify, according to the contract). Keep copies of all documents and your policy.
Step 4: Verifying eligibility for subsidies
If your income is low, apply for premium reduction at the social welfare office of Canton Fribourg. Be prepared with your tax return, bank statements, and a copy of your LAMal policy. Renewal deadlines for subsidies are generally in November/December for the following year.
### Useful tools and contacts
To find insurance companies operating in Fribourg and compare premiums, you can use the national comparison tool from the Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH) or directly consult the websites of major insurers. For information about subsidies specific to Canton Fribourg, contact the competent cantonal office (exact name: check on the canton's official website).
It's also useful to use an evaluation tool to estimate your expected annual medical expenses and check what deductible value is most convenient for your situation. [Try our healthcare cost calculator](nav:health) for a personalized assessment.
Remember: LAMal is essential protection in Switzerland. Maintaining continuous coverage avoids penalties and ensures access to healthcare services without unexpected financial risks. Those who fail to obtain health insurance within the required 3 months face a cantonal administrative fine, which can amount to several hundred francs. Additionally, insurance companies can recover costs for healthcare services received during the period without coverage, a significant financial burden. To avoid this situation, take action immediately after moving.

item.title: Opening a business in Zug: trade register and costs
item.description: Canton of Zug: legal forms, federal minimum capital, cantonal registration fees, AVS, LAINF and operational steps to start a business.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Opening a business in Switzerland requires registration in the commercial register of the canton - The choice of legal form determines capital, liability and accounting obligations - Minimum capital and registration fees vary depending on the business form - Insurance and pension obligations commence from the start of the business
## Key Facts - **What**: Starting a business in the Canton of Zugo, with registration in the commercial register - When: Current period - Where: Canton of Zugo, Switzerland - Who: Aspiring entrepreneurs, individuals and legal entities - Amount: Minimum capital according to the chosen legal form (details to be verified with the commercial register office) - Fees: Registration costs determined by the cantonal commercial register office - Insurance: Obligation to have AVS/AI/IPG, AD and LAINF coverage from the first employee
Starting a business in the Canton of Zugo requires a series of mandatory steps that begin with the choice of legal form. This decision determines the amount of minimum capital, the liability regime and accounting obligations. In Switzerland, the most common forms are sole proprietorship, general partnership, limited partnership, joint-stock company (SA) and limited liability company (SAGL).
### The Choice of Legal Form The sole proprietorship is the simplest form: it is registered in the commercial register only if annual turnover exceeds a certain threshold set by law. It does not require minimum capital, but the owner is liable for debts with their own assets. The general partnership and limited partnership involve two or more people, with unlimited liability for the partners.
The SA and SAGL are the most structured forms. The SAGL requires a minimum capital set by law and the SA requires a minimum capital set by law: both amounts are defined at the federal level and apply uniformly throughout Switzerland. The difference between the two cantons therefore cannot concern the minimum capital threshold, but possibly the administrative registration costs.
### Registration at the Zugo Commercial Register Registration in the commercial register is handled by the competent cantonal office. For individuals, registration is mandatory when the business reaches a certain size; for legal entities (SA, SAGL), registration is always mandatory. The procedure includes the submission of the articles of association or partnership agreement, the identification of the founders and the payment of capital.
The registration fees are determined by the commercial register office of the Canton of Zugo and vary depending on the legal form and the complexity of the matter. To get an up-to-date picture, it is advisable to consult the official cantonal website or the competent office directly, as the amounts may be subject to periodic revisions. Opening a business in the Canton of Zug involves a series of practical implications that go beyond simple registration in the commercial register. Swiss taxation is structured at three levels — federal direct tax (FDT), cantonal tax and municipal tax — and each canton has its own tax law and its own multiplier. Municipalities apply an additional multiplier to cantonal tax.
### Taxation and accounting obligations For those starting a business in Zug, the FDT is managed by the Federal Tax Administration (FTA/ESTV), while cantonal and municipal taxes fall under the responsibility of the cantonal tax administration. VAT, when the business reaches the expected thresholds, is also administered by the FTA/ESTV. It is not the task of FSIO/BSV to set tax rates: that federal office is responsible for social security (AVS, AI, LPP).
The choice of legal form affects the tax regime: a sole proprietorship is taxed based on the personal income of the owner, while SA and SAGL are subject to profit tax. In Zug, as in the rest of Switzerland, the municipal multiplier varies from one municipality to another, affecting the overall tax burden.
### Costs and comparisons between legal forms The minimum capital required varies significantly depending on the form chosen. For a sole proprietorship, no minimum capital is required. For an LLC, federal law provides for a specific minimum capital, while for a corporation, the minimum capital is set by federal law at a higher level. These amounts are identical in all cantons and do not change in Zug compared to Zurich, Geneva or Basel.
The fees for registering in the commercial register are, however, under cantonal jurisdiction and can therefore differ from one canton to another. Notary costs, when required for the formation of a corporation or LLC, also vary based on the cantonal fee schedule. For an entrepreneur comparing Zug to other cantons, the main difference lies in the tax rates and municipal multipliers, not in capital requirements.
### Insurance and pension obligations From the moment the business is started and there are employees, a series of contribution obligations are triggered. AVS/AI/DI contributions amount to 10.6% of salary (5.3% borne by the employee and 5.3% borne by the employer). AD/AC contributions are equal to 1.1% up to the annual maximum provided. LAINF/LAA, managed by SUVA for most sectors, ranges from 0.7% to 1.5% of salary depending on the business sector.
If the business is started as an employer, it is necessary to affiliate with the competent AVS compensation fund and take out insurance against occupational and non-occupational accidents. For those operating as self-employed without employees, the obligation to affiliate with a compensation fund remains, with the possibility of choosing the most appropriate contribution class.
### Health insurance and individual obligations The business owner, as a resident of Switzerland, is subject to the obligation to take out health insurance according to LAMal within three months of arrival or when the right arises. Premiums are private, per capita, and do not constitute a salary contribution. Deductibles of the adult's choice start from CHF 300 and reach up to CHF 2500, with intermediate amounts of CHF 500, 1000, 1500 and 2000. Premiums vary by canton and region, and the Canton of Zug provides a premium reduction (subsidy) for low incomes.
From the point of view of rental, anyone who starts a business in Zug and needs commercial premises is subject to the federal provisions of the Code of Obligations (art. 253 et seq. CO): the security deposit cannot exceed three months' rent and must be held in an account in the tenant's name; the landlord's notice is valid only on the official cantonal form; any objection must be filed within thirty days with the conciliation authority.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Step-by-step procedure to open a business in Zug
1. **Define the legal form**. Evaluate the pros and cons of sole proprietorship, joint-stock company, limited liability company or other forms, considering capital, liability and tax regime.
2. Check the need for capital. For joint-stock companies and limited liability companies, the minimum capital is set by federal law; for sole proprietorships, no minimum capital is required. For capital companies, capital must be paid in and deposited before registration.
3. Prepare the articles of incorporation or partnership agreement. The articles of incorporation of a joint-stock company or limited liability company must contain the company name, registered office, purpose, capital and corporate bodies. It can be drafted independently or with the assistance of a notary.
4. Register with the commercial register. Submit the documentation to the commercial register office of the Canton of Zug. Registration fees vary depending on the legal form: for current amounts it is advisable to consult the official website of the canton.
5. Tax registration. Notify the cantonal tax authority of the commencement of business activities and, where applicable, the Federal Tax Administration for federal direct tax and VAT. The VAT declaration must be filed if turnover exceeds the thresholds provided by law.
6. Affiliation with the AVS compensation fund. Mandatory for both employers and self-employed individuals. AVS/AI/IPG contributions start at 5.3% borne by the employee (10.6% total including the employer).
7. Accident insurance (accident insurance law). Take out a policy with SUVA or a recognized private insurer, depending on the sector of activity. The premium varies between 0.7% and 1.5% of salary.
8. Health insurance (health insurance law). The owner and employees must take out coverage within three months. The deductible can be chosen between CHF 300, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000 or 2500.
9. Occupational pension (occupational pension law). If employees are hired with salaries subject to occupational pension law, affiliation with a pension fund is mandatory. Minimum contributions on coordinated salary are 7% (25-34 years), 10% (35-44), 15% (45-54) and 18% (55+ until retirement age).
10. Work permits for foreign citizens. If the entrepreneur is not Swiss, they must verify their permit (L short-term residence, B temporary residence, C permanent residence, G cross-border commuter) with the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM). Starting a business may require a specific authorization depending on the type of permit.
### Subsequent deadlines and obligations After registration, the business is subject to recurring obligations: periodic VAT declaration, declaration of cantonal and federal taxes, payment of pension contributions and submission of annual accounts (for joint-stock companies and limited liability companies). Bookkeeping can be entrusted to an authorized accounting firm.
### Useful tools To get oriented on costs and current tax rates, it is advisable to consult directly the website of the Canton of Zug and that of the Federal Tax Administration. To simulate the impact of taxes and pension contributions on your income, the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) is available, a tool that allows you to estimate the net from the gross and applicable contributions.
For those who want to deepen knowledge on real estate taxation and property taxes, the subject of [tax return](nav:tax-return) is a mandatory step for every new business. Finally, to assess the [cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living) — rent, health insurance premiums, transportation — before starting a business in Zug, it is useful to consult the most recent available data.

item.title: Jans and Dobrindt: CH-Germany border cooperation
item.description: August 31, 2026: Chiasso. Federal Councillor and German Minister agree on strengthening cross-border cooperation. Proposal for a Police-Doganale Cooperation Centre. Asylum and stops are decreasing.
item.content:encoded:
## In short - Jans-Dobrindt meeting in Chiasso for cross-border security cooperation - Proposal for creation of Police-Customs Cooperation Centre at CH-Germany border - Arrests for illegal residence and asylum applications continue to decline - EU Migration Pact in force since June 12, 2026
## Key facts - **What**: Agreement on cross-border security and migration cooperation - When: August 31, 2026 - Where: Chiasso, Switzerland-Italy/Germany border - Who: Beat Jans (Federal Councillor), Alexander Dobrindt (German Interior Minister) - Proposals: Police-Customs Cooperation Centre (PCCC) or conversion of Basel office - EU Pact: Entered into force June 12, 2026 - Trend: Asylum applications and arrests for illegal residence declining
On August 31, 2026, in Chiasso, Federal Councillor Beat Jans met with German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt for crucial discussions on border security and cross-border police cooperation. The meeting, held right at the Swiss border, represented a moment of administrative convergence between the two Governments aimed at strengthening the fight against crime and irregular migration.
During the meeting, the two ministers agreed to examine various options for deepening collaboration. One involves the creation of a Police and Customs Cooperation Centre (PCCC) directly at the border between Switzerland and Germany. The alternative is the conversion of the current liaison office in Basel, already a point of contact between the two countries from which to coordinate joint operations. The stated objective is to improve information exchange between the security authorities of the two States, allowing faster and more coordinated responses to transnational criminal phenomena.
### Migration situation: positive signals
Jans and Dobrindt also discussed the course of migration at Switzerland's southern and northern borders. According to the official federal statement, both arrests for illegal residence and asylum applications submitted in both countries continue to decline. A positive trend that highlights how the collaborative measures already adopted are producing measurable effects.
The two ministers place further hopes in the implementation of the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum, which entered into force on June 12, 2026. This European regulatory instrument should produce even more positive effects on migration policy in the coming months, creating synergies between EU countries and neighbouring countries such as Switzerland.
### Historical collaboration between Switzerland and Germany
Jans and Dobrindt paid tribute to the long and close collaboration already existing between the two countries, focused on combating crime and irregular migration. This cooperation, consolidated over the years, represents a model of administrative integration pursued with a view to shared security. The two ministers reiterated their commitment to strengthening it further, recognizing that strengthening common borders is an objective of mutual interest and regional stability. ## Implications for those who work and reside in Switzerland
The strengthened cooperation between Switzerland and Germany will have direct repercussions on migration management and cross-border mobility. For those who live or work in Switzerland, especially near the borders, this means potentially more efficient procedures at border offices and more thorough control of irregular migration. The decline in detentions for illegal stay and in asylum applications, reported during the meeting, suggests that the measures already in place are producing positive effects. The implementation of a CCPD at the border with Germany, if confirmed, could further accelerate this trend by allowing Swiss and German authorities to coordinate controls in real time and exchange data more quickly.
### Effects on the labour market and cross-border mobility
One of the sectors most sensitive to these changes is that of cross-border workers. Switzerland, although outside the European Union, depends on bilateral agreements to regulate the entry of foreign workers. Stricter control of irregular migration, a direct consequence of enhanced cooperation, helps maintain a clear distinction between the regular entry of authorised workers and unauthorised migration. This administrative order is essential to preserve the balance of the national labour market.
For those who regularly cross the border in search of employment or to carry out legitimate work, more efficient border management translates into greater predictability in crossing procedures. The [Swiss labour market](nav:jobs) remains open to regular foreign workers, but CH-Germany cooperation reinforces the filtering mechanisms against crime and illegal employment.
### The role of the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum
The EU Pact on Migration and Asylum, which entered into force on 12 June 2026, acts as a catalyst for these cooperation efforts. Although Switzerland is not an EU member, it remains indirectly influenced by European regulations due to its geographical proximity and economic interdependence. A more orderly managed migration at European level entails, by extension, a more regulated migration also entering Swiss territory. Ministers Jans and Dobrindt expect the implementation of the Pact to produce further positive effects on the reduction of unfounded asylum applications and irregular entry attempts.
### Efficiency of controls and impact on security
The creation of a CCPD or the transformation of the liaison office in Basel represent concrete operational tools to improve real-time information exchange. When properly implemented, these mechanisms reduce the response times of police and customs authorities, creating a deterrent effect against illegal trafficking and transnational crime. For regular workers and residents in Switzerland, this translates into safer borders and crossing procedures that, while remaining rigorous, are more efficient and predictable.

item.title: Swiss cities: more margin for climate and 30 km/h on the roads
item.description: SKM and the Union of Cities call on Bern and the Cantons not to obstruct zones 30 and call for a national "polluter pays" strategy.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Swiss cities are calling for more leeway on climate adaptation - Heat waves: fewer impervious surfaces, more greenery - 30 km/h speed limit indicated as a key measure - Demand for a national 'polluter pays' strategy
## Key facts - **What**: Cities are calling for greater room for manoeuvre on climate adaptation measures on urban roads - When: Statement released today by the Conference of Cities for Mobility (SKM); exact date not specified - Where: Switzerland, particularly the urban centres represented by the Swiss Union of Cities - Who: Conference of Cities for Mobility (SKM), convened within the transport departments; Swiss Union of Cities - Climate context: Increasingly frequent heat waves, which make adaptation measures necessary - Measures indicated: Reduction of impervious surfaces, creation of more green spaces, 30 km/h speed limit - Further demand: A national strategy for traffic pricing based on the 'polluter pays' principle - Political criticism: The Confederation and several Cantons have allegedly hindered the introduction of the 30 km/h limit in recent years
Switzerland's cities are calling for more decision-making space to implement climate adaptation measures on urban roads. This emerges from the position paper released by the heads of the transport departments gathered in the Conference of Cities for Mobility (SKM), which refers to the Swiss Union of Cities.
The starting point is the recurring heat waves, a phenomenon that, according to the cities, requires structural interventions on the urban fabric: in particular, the reduction of impervious surfaces and the creation of more green spaces. The statement explicitly indicates as a 'key measure' also a reduction of the speed limit to 30 km/h.
### Political obstacles complained of by the cities
The SKM denounces that the Confederation and several Cantons have allegedly hindered the introduction of the 30 km/h limit in recent years. For this reason, the Conference urges the federal and cantonal authorities 'not to further complicate or block the relevant projects'.
In addition to the speed issue, the Conference of Cities for Mobility is calling for a national strategy for traffic pricing based on the 'polluter pays' principle. The SKM also indicates as determining factors, alongside the reduction of speed, the reduction of individual motorised traffic and a greater shared use of vehicles. Swiss cities are once again calling for broader decision-making powers on a dossier that intertwines traffic, public health and urban planning. The request comes from the Conference of Cities for Mobility (SKM), which brings together the heads of urban transport offices, in coordination with the Swiss Union of Cities.
The political issue raised by the cities concerns the relationship with Bern and the Cantons. According to the SKM, in recent years the introduction of the 30 km/h speed limit has been hindered both by the Confederation and by several Cantons. The Conference now explicitly demands that 'the federal and cantonal authorities do not further complicate or block the relevant projects'.
### The measures put on the table
The SKM note identifies three main lines of action:
- climate adaptation on urban roads, with a reduction of impervious surfaces and an increase in green areas; - a 30 km/h speed limit as a 'key measure'; - a reduction in individual motorized traffic and greater shared use of vehicles.
On the latter point, the Conference calls for a national strategy for traffic pricing based on the 'polluter pays' principle, a formulation reported verbatim in the note.
### Institutional levels involved
The cities' request operates on three levels: federal (for a national pricing strategy), cantonal (on the authorization of speed limits) and municipal (on the concrete management of roads and green spaces). In Switzerland, competences regarding road signage and speed are divided between the Confederation, the Cantons and the Municipalities, and the Conference of Cities for Mobility aims to obtain a greater operational margin for the Municipalities, which are currently subject to cantonal and federal scrutiny.
From a political-economic standpoint, the dossier touches on issues that affect both residents and commuters: air quality in urban areas, management of public space, traffic organization and, at the federal level, any national mechanisms for mobility pricing.

The position taken by the Conference of Cities for Mobility (SKM) opens a political pathway that may closely concern those who live and work in Swiss urban areas. For now, this is a political request, not an already approved measure: the Conference is asking federal and cantonal authorities not to hinder projects and is calling for a national traffic pricing strategy based on the 'polluter pays' principle.
### What changes, in concrete terms
If the cities' requests were to be accepted, the potential effects concern three distinct areas:
- Speed limits: municipalities could have more leeway to introduce 30 km/h zones, currently subject, according to the SKM, to obstacles from the Confederation and the Cantons. - Urban spaces: cities could expand green surfaces and reduce impervious ones, indications explicitly contained in the note. - Mobility and tariffs: the Conference is calling for a national strategy for traffic pricing based on the 'polluter pays' principle, without further operational details in the note.
### What to do in the meantime
For residents, workers, and commuters who wish to follow the evolution of the dossier, the operational steps are still being defined at the federal and cantonal level. Pending developments, it is useful to:
- check on your municipality's website for any 30 km/h zone projects already launched or under consultation; - follow the communications of the cantonal transport departments, which are responsible for reviewing local speed limits; - monitor the position statements of the Swiss Union of Cities and the SKM, which represent the common front of cities on this dossier.

item.title: Gender pay gap: reduced to 15.7%
item.description: The wage gap between women and men in Switzerland continues to narrow. In 2024 it stands at 15.7%, down from 16.2% in 2022. The UST report of August 31, 2026 analyzes the data by sector and role.
item.content:encoded:
## At a glance - Overall wage gap at 15.7% in 2024 - Down from 16.2% in 2022 and from 19% in 2018 - Unexplained portion of 6.5%, equal to 640 francs less per month
## Key facts - **What**: FSO report on wage structure and gender gap - When: 31 August 2026 (data referring to 2024) - Where: Whole of Switzerland, private and public sectors - Who: Federal Statistical Office (FSO) - Amount: 15.7% overall gap; 640 francs/month of unexplained difference - Trend: Progressive reduction from 19% in 2018
The Federal Statistical Office published on 31 August 2026 the detailed analysis of the wage gap between women and men in Switzerland, based on the Swiss wage structure survey 2024. The results confirm a positive trend consolidated over time: the overall wage gap stands at 15.7%, down from 16.2% in 2022, 18% in 2020 and 19% in 2018.
Women earned on average 15.7% less than their male colleagues, calculated on standardized gross monthly wages equivalent to full-time (100%) based on actual working time. In the private sector, the gap reaches 17.2% in 2024, slightly down from 17.5% in 2022, 19.5% in 2020 and 19.6% in 2018. In the public sector (Confederation, Cantons and Municipalities considered as a whole), the general wage gap stands at 12.8% in 2024, down from 13.8% in 2022, 15.1% in 2020 and 18.1% in 2018.
However, wage disparities are not solely due to easily explainable factors such as level of education, years of service or hierarchical function. The FSO distinguishes between a portion of the gap attributable to these structural differences and an 'unexplained' portion that remains difficult to justify. In 2024, the unexplained portion of the gap at the overall level stands at 6.5%, equivalent to 640 gross francs per month (it was 7%, equal to 657 francs in 2022).
### Significant disparities by economic branch
Analyzing the private sector by economic branch, very significant disparities emerge. In the accommodation and food services branch, women earned 7.9% less than men. In retail trade, the gap rises to 16.9%. In the manufacture of machinery and equipment, it reaches 17.2%. In the financial and insurance activities branch, the gap widens dramatically to 30.6%, the highest value among all sectors analyzed.
The unexplained portion of the gap also varies considerably across sectors. In the accommodation and food services branch, it corresponds to 191 francs per month. In retail trade, it reaches 606 francs. In the manufacture of machinery, it rises to 829 francs. In the financial and insurance activities branch, the unexplained disparity is the most marked: 1,506 francs per month.
In the private sector as a whole, the unexplained portion of the gap stands at 6.7% in 2024 (7.2% in 2022), corresponding to 644 francs per month (653 francs in 2022). In the public sector, the unexplained wage gap in 2024 is equal to 5.9%, or on average 574 francs per month (6.7% and 623 francs in 2022). ### Company size amplifies the gap
The unexplained pay gap varies significantly depending on company size. In small businesses with fewer than 20 employees, it reaches 8.6% in 2024 (8.4% in 2022). In large companies with at least 1000 employees, it drops to 5.8% in 2024 (6.8% in 2022). This pattern suggests that larger companies, likely equipped with more structured and transparent pay processes, tend to reduce gender gaps that are difficult to explain through objective factors such as qualifications or experience.
### Corporate hierarchy: the multiplier factor
Hierarchical position has a marked effect on the unexplained gap. Among employees without a managerial role, the unexplained portion of the gap is 6.1% in 2024 (6.6% in 2022). Among employees with a senior managerial role, the disparity jumps to 12.4% in 2024 (10.6% in 2022). This doubling of the gap when moving from operational levels to company leadership reflects a concerning trend: the higher up the hierarchy, the greater the pay gap that is difficult to justify by differences in role, formal skills or responsibilities.
### Age and family status: critical variables
Age significantly amplifies the unexplained gap. Women under 30 earned, on average, 2.2% less than men with the same structural characteristics (2.4% in 2022). Women over 50 instead earned 8.3% less than their male peers (8.5% in 2022). The gap practically doubles between young and older workers, suggesting that pay disparities accumulate and amplify over the course of a career.
Marital status and family situation have an equally considerable impact on the unexplained disparity. Among single employees, the unexplained gap is 2.7% in 2024 (2.8% in 2022). Among married employees, it jumps to 8.1% (8.8% in 2022). However, the FSO explicitly emphasises that, although marital status and family situation may be informative for describing pay gaps, according to the Federal Act on Gender Equality (SR 151.1), such characteristics must NOT be used to justify gender pay disparities.
### Professional education: a protective factor
The level of education significantly affects the unexplained portion of the gap. Among employees who graduated from a university of applied sciences or a teachers' college, the unexplained gap is 3.8% in 2024 (3.5% in 2022), the lowest value among all education levels analysed. Employees with vocational training record an unexplained gap of 6.6% in 2024 (7.3% in 2022). These data suggest that a professionalising university education may offer relative protection against gender pay disparities that are difficult to explain.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Where to find the complete data
The detailed report from the Federal Statistical Office on the 2024 Swiss Salary Structure Survey contains the full analysis of the wage gap between women and men. The official press release, published on 31 August 2026, provides the aggregate figures, historical trends since 2018, and the main variables influencing the gap (sector, company size, hierarchical role, age, education, marital status).
### How to use this data in practice
For those working in Switzerland, this data provides an important benchmark for evaluating your own salary situation. If you are a woman and notice a significant discrepancy compared to male colleagues performing the same role, you can use this report as documentary evidence in discussions with your employer or when contacting trade unions and gender equality bodies. The FSO data shows that gaps of 6-7% (the unexplained portion) cannot be attributed to differences in skills or experience, suggesting possible forms of wage discrimination.
### Positive trend but persistent concerns
The FSO data confirms that the trend of reducing the wage gap continues year after year. From 19% in 2018 to 15.7% in 2024 represents tangible progress of 3.3 percentage points over six years. However, significant concerns remain, particularly in senior management (12.4% unexplained) and in financial activities (30.6% overall gap). Monitoring this data annually remains essential to assess whether the pay equity policies undertaken by companies and the public sector are actually reducing the gap.

item.title: UBS: new banking rules, the Commission's compromise
item.description: 31 August 2026: CET-S approves stricter rules on foreign holdings of large banks, with 50% coverage in AT1 instead of 100% as proposed by the Federal Council.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - The Economic Affairs Committee of the Council of States approves stricter rules for systemic banks (primarily UBS) - Compromise: 50% coverage with CET-1 own funds + 50% with AT1 bonds - Vote: 10 in favour, 2 against; the decision is not 'a gift to UBS' - Currently, a capital coverage of 60% applies to foreign participations
## Key facts - **What**: New rules on foreign participations of systemic banks - When: 31 August 2026 - Where: Economic Affairs and Taxation Committee of the Council of States (Bern) - Who: CET-S (chairman Erich Ettlin, Centre/OW) - Amount: 50% coverage in CET-1 + 50% in AT1 (vs. federal proposal of 100% CET-1) - Votes: 10 in favour, 2 against
### The Committee's decision
Bern, 31 August 2026. The Economic Affairs and Taxation Committee of the Council of States (CET-S) has approved a new regulation on foreign participations of large Swiss banks. According to the committee, systemic institutions — currently mainly UBS — must be subject to stricter rules on the coverage of these investments, but not at the level required by the Federal Council.
The Federal Council had proposed a coverage requirement of 100% through Common Equity Tier 1 (CET-1) own funds. The CET-S opted for a compromise: banks will cover half of their foreign participations with CET-1 own funds, and the other half through so-called AT1 bonds (Additional Tier 1). These are hybrid instruments that offer a high yield and can be converted into equity or declared worthless in the event of the company's distress — a scenario similar to what happened during the Credit Suisse crisis.
The committee vote recorded 10 votes in favour and 2 against. CET-S chairman Erich Ettlin (Centre/OW) stressed at a press conference that the decision represents 'a compromise' and not a gift to UBS. The purchase of AT1 entails costs for the bank, but Ettlin specified that the amount of such costs remains to be defined. The bank itself had strongly opposed the government proposal.
Today, banks must maintain capital coverage of 60% for foreign participations. The new rule would raise this level, although it does not reach the total requirement requested by the Federal Council. Ettlin also communicated that the Committee was unable to examine the Public Liquidity Backstop mechanism during its work.
### Balancing protection and competitiveness
According to Ettlin, the Committee's choice aims to 'strengthen the rules to better protect taxpayers, but also to ensure that the economy is not subject to excessive regulation'. This balance is central to the debate on Swiss banking supervision: on the one hand, the need to protect the financial system and savers from systemic risks; on the other, the concern that overly restrictive rules could compromise the international competitiveness of Swiss institutions. ### What AT1 Bonds Are and Why They Matter
To understand the CET-S compromise, one must first clarify the nature of AT1 bonds. Unlike Common Equity Tier-1 (CET-1) capital, which represents the most stable core capital of a bank, AT1 instruments are hybrid securities. They offer interest rates higher than conventional bonds, but they carry significant risks for those who hold them.
During the Credit Suisse crisis, AT1 bonds were declared worthless — a rare event that concretely demonstrated how these instruments do not guarantee capital safety. In the event of a bank's difficulties, the investor holding AT1s may lose it all, or see them converted into shares with drastically reduced value. This is why their use as a form of capital coverage is controversial: they do not offer the same level of protection as CET-1.
The Federal Council's proposal (100% CET-1) was more stringent and would have required UBS to accumulate significant amounts of capital as reserves. The Commission, on the other hand, considered that partial recourse to AT1s would allow a balance between two competing needs: maintaining prudential oversight over liquidity and capital stability, without forcing the bank to retain abnormally large volumes of CET-1 — resources it could otherwise deploy in profitable activities.
### Implications for the National Banking System
This decision primarily concerns UBS, but it signals a broader stance by the Swiss supervisory authorities. The Council of States (and by extension the Swiss Parliament) intends to tighten the discipline on systemically important banks without, however, strangling them with excessive constraints. The Commission chose to also involve market instruments (the AT1s) within the perimeter of protection, entrusting the market with the pricing of the associated risks.
For savers and investors, this choice carries a dual implication. On the one hand, more stringent rules on foreign participations reduce the likelihood that a large bank will accumulate massive losses on foreign investments without adequate coverage. On the other, the use of AT1s introduces an element of uncertainty: those who hold these securities know that, in a severe banking crisis scenario, their investment could be wiped out or converted into shares at nominal value.
The current coverage level (60%, which the Commission intended to raise) represented a previous compromise. With the new rules — still to be approved in plenary session — the parameter will rise, better protecting the system from uncovered exposures. However, the fact that UBS is not required to cover 100% with CET-1 means that the bank will retain a certain flexibility in managing its balance sheet and investment strategies.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### What savers and investors need to know
This decision by the CET-S will have a long-term effect, as it still needs to be approved by the full Council of States and may be subject to further modifications. However, anyone holding deposits at UBS or owning Swiss bank securities should keep a few elements in mind.
First: the new rule is aimed at better protecting depositors from risks related to uncovered foreign participations. If applied, the rules will reduce the bank's unsecured exposure, which theoretically increases the security of deposits within the Swiss system. Second: if you hold AT1 instruments issued by UBS or other systemically important banks, be aware that the value of these instruments depends on the solvency of the issuing bank. In a financial stress scenario, the value of AT1 instruments can collapse or be wiped out, as happened with Credit Suisse.
Third: CET-S decisions reflect a global trend towards greater rigour in banking supervision. This is not an isolated phenomenon in Switzerland, but part of an international orientation. If you work in the financial sector, the new rules will entail stricter compliance requirements and demand close attention to internal risk management processes.
### Next steps and what to monitor
The Commission's decision, although important, is not yet law. The text must be submitted to the full Council of States for final approval. After the Council of States, the procedure will follow the ordinary legislative paths, possibly including a meeting with the National Council (the lower house of the Swiss Parliament). Further modifications may emerge during this process.
Ettlin also pointed out that the Commission did not have time to examine the Public Liquidity Backstop mechanism, an issue closely related to the protection of banking stability. This topic could return to the agenda in the future.
If you are a saver or investor interested in the dynamics of the Swiss financial sector, it is worth monitoring parliamentary developments over the coming months. You can consult the Swiss Parliament website or the official Confederation portal to follow the legislative process. In the meantime, if you hold AT1 instruments or other hybrid securities, assess the risk profile together with a qualified financial advisor. For broader planning of your wealth and pension situation, [use our financial planning calculator](nav:calculator) to analyse how your investment choices align with your long-term goals.
Finally, remember that decisions on banking supervision also indirectly affect bank competitiveness and profits, which in turn impact dividends and returns for shareholders. If you hold UBS shares, stay informed on how the new capital constraints could redefine the bank's capital return strategy. [Explore your banking investment options in Switzerland](nav:banks) to better orient yourself in the market.

item.title: Record income and savings in Switzerland in 2025
item.description: In 2025, the disposable income per inhabitant exceeds CHF 65,000. Voluntary savings rate at 19.3%, all-time high. UST data reveals the highest economic well-being ever.
item.content:encoded:
## At a glance - In 2025, disposable income per inhabitant exceeds 65,000 CHF (all-time high) - Voluntary savings rate reaches 19.3% for the first time - Growth of +36% since 1995 at purchasing power parity - Source: Federal Statistical Office (FSO)
## Key facts - **What**: Disposable income and voluntary savings reach all-time highs - When: 2025 - Where: Switzerland (national average) - Who: Federal Statistical Office (FSO) - Amount: 65,124 CHF per inhabitant (disposable income) - Savings rate: 19.3% voluntary, 27.4% overall - Growth 1995-2025: 36% net of inflation
For the first time, adjusted disposable income per inhabitant has exceeded 65,000 francs and the voluntary savings rate of households has reached 19.3%, an all-time high in the series. The Federal Statistical Office has published official data on the financial situation of Swiss households for 2025, and the figures are striking for their absolute records.
Adjusted disposable income per inhabitant reached exactly 65,124 CHF in 2025. In the same year, the voluntary savings rate hit 19.3%, a level never recorded before in the entire FSO historical series. These figures do not represent a one-off anomaly, but rather the confirmation of a multi-decade trend of steady growth.
Over the past thirty years, adjusted disposable income per inhabitant has grown uninterruptedly. Since 1995, when it stood at 40,083 francs, growth at purchasing power parity reaches almost 36%. The average purchasing power of the Swiss today is therefore well above that of a generation ago.
### How disposable income is measured
Adjusted disposable income of households per inhabitant is a fundamental economic indicator used to measure the material well-being and real purchasing power of citizens. It represents how much money remains with families after adding up all incomes and subtracting current taxes and social contributions, and adding the value of free or subsidised public services that citizens benefit from. This metric offers a much more accurate picture of the quality of life compared to the traditional gross disposable income.
The increase in housing costs, health insurance premiums and other mandatory expenses continues, however, to weigh on many Swiss households. Differences between regions, income brackets and types of households remain significant. Nevertheless, looking at the population as a whole, the long-term trend appears clear and unequivocal. ## The growth of savings: a singular phenomenon
Income growth is important, but the peculiarity that emerges when observing the behaviour of households is even more significant. While in many European countries the increase in income mainly translates into a growth in consumption, in Switzerland a growing share of resources is regularly set aside.
In 2025, the overall savings rate reached 27.4% of adjusted gross disposable income, compared with 19.6% in 1995. This means that more than a quarter of the resources available to households is allocated to the formation of savings. Every person living in Switzerland spent approximately 53,000 francs and set aside almost 18,000 francs, of which around 12,600 in the form of voluntary savings.
### The record of voluntary savings
For the first time in the history of data published by the FSO, the voluntary savings rate reached 19.3% in 2025, almost double the 9.7% recorded thirty years earlier. Voluntary savings represent the share that remains after considering not only consumption, but also the mandatory saving components linked to the pension system, such as contributions to the LPP occupational pension fund.
This figure shows a concrete and not merely theoretical financial capacity. Swiss households not only earn more, but also have ever greater margins to accumulate wealth, deal with unforeseen events and plan for the future with greater peace of mind.
### The effect of the pandemic and the persistence of the trend
The pandemic marked a turning point in the national propensity to save. After a phase of moderate growth between the end of the 1990s and the first decade of the 2000s, the propensity to save began to strengthen gradually starting from 2020. The limitations on consumption imposed by health measures led to an increase in household savings, a classic mechanism in periods of economic and social uncertainty.
However, once the health emergency came over, there was no return to previous levels. Savings continued to rise significantly, a sign of a financial capacity that has consolidated over the years. Financial crises, recessions, geopolitical tensions and a pandemic have not weakened the propensity to save, but have structurally strengthened it.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## How to leverage greater savings capacity
For Swiss families, access to an increasingly higher disposable income combined with a well-established propensity to save creates concrete opportunities for long-term financial planning. However, it is essential to act strategically: setting money aside without a clear direction is very different from building a structured savings plan based on specific goals.
The three priority areas are: pension planning through contributions to the LPP (pension fund), which remains the foundation of the Swiss pension system; optimisation of Pillar 3a, which offers significant tax benefits every year up to a defined maximum amount that can be deducted from the [tax return](nav:tax-return); and building a solid family budget to identify where to direct savings toward concrete goals such as retirement, emergencies, and purchasing a home.
### Key procedures and deadlines for savings
Each canton has slightly different rules regarding Pillar 3a, but at the federal level the deadlines remain uniform and well known. The annual tax return is the crucial moment to verify whether you are fully exploiting the deduction tools available for retirement savings. Many Swiss residents do not take full advantage of tax benefits at the cantonal and federal levels.
If you are an employee, the [family budget calculator](nav:calculator) allows you to simulate the impact of your pension contributions on gross disposable income and identify margins for optimisation. For self-employed individuals or those with diversified income, consulting a cantonal tax advisor remains useful to avoid missing structured savings and estate planning opportunities.
### Using data to plan the future
FSO data show that there is concrete room to save in Switzerland: the key now is to direct it toward specific goals rather than letting it be dispersed in everyday consumption. Use [our pension planning tools](nav:pension) and the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to simulate your options and start planning your future financial well-being today.
