item.title: Swiss banks, the CET-S restrains the Federal Council on equity capital
item.description: The Commission of the Council of States modifies the government's proposal: up to half of the coverage may come from AT1 bonds, not just from CET-1.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - CET-S slows down the 100% coverage in own funds for foreign subsidiaries - AT1 bonds could cover half of the required coverage - Currently the capital coverage for foreign participations is 60% - UBS is the only systemic bank today affected by the measure
## Key facts - **What**: The Commission for Economics and Taxes of the Council of States (CET-S) amends the Federal Council's proposal on the coverage of foreign participations of systemic banks - When: Debate and vote in Commission, announcement made in the evening via press conference - Where: Bern, Federal Palace - Who: CET-S, chaired by Erich Ettlin (Centre/OW); Federal Councillor Karin Keller-Sutter (Federal Department of Finance, FDF); Daniela Stoffel (State Secretariat for International Finance Matters, SIF) - How: Vote with 10 in favour, 2 against and 1 abstention - Original proposal: 100% coverage through Common Equity Tier 1 own funds (CET-1) - CET-S proposal: Partial coverage through AT1 bonds (Additional Tier 1), with a revision of their functioning - Current regime: Capital coverage of 60% for foreign participations
The Commission for Economics and Taxes of the Council of States (CET-S) has decided not to impose on the large Swiss banks a full 100% coverage in Common Equity Tier 1 own funds (CET-1) for their foreign subsidiaries, as proposed by the Federal Council within the framework of the revision of the banking law. The Commission prefers instead to allow about half of the coverage to be guaranteed through the so-called AT1 bonds (Additional Tier 1), hybrid instruments that offer a high yield but that can be converted into own capital or declared worthless in the event of difficulties of the issuing company — a mechanism that became known to the general public during the Credit Suisse affair.
The CET-S however requests a revision of the AT1 bonds, so that their loss-absorption effect is quicker. Measures are also envisaged aimed at preventing a bank from issuing these securities when it is already in a precarious financial situation, to avoid that the rescue instrument itself becomes a source of risk.
### Own capital and consequences in case of failure to meet the requirements
The CET-S has also defined what happens if a bank should no longer be able to meet the 'hard' own capital requirements. In these cases, the obligation to suspend the payment of dividends to shareholders and the repurchase of shares will kick in. The bonuses paid to executives will have to be reduced, or even suppressed, depending on the extent and duration of the failure to meet the capital requirements. The decision was taken at the end of a debate held in the presence of Federal Councillor Karin Keller-Sutter, head of the Federal Department of Finance (FDF), and of Daniela Stoffel, head of the State Secretariat for International Finance Matters (SIF). The final vote recorded 10 in favour, 2 against and 1 abstention. The Commission did not have time to examine the state Public Liquidity Backstop mechanism, a topic that remains open. ### The reasons for the compromise: why not 100% CET-1
CET-S President Erich Ettlin summarized the philosophy behind the decision with an explicit formula: 'We want to strengthen the rules to better protect taxpayers, but also to ensure that the economy is not subjected to excessive regulation.' It is a balance between two needs: on the one hand, the protection of financial stability and public funds; on the other, the preservation of the international competitiveness of the Swiss financial center. Ettlin then made clear that this is 'a compromise — and not a gift to UBS': the purchase of AT1 bonds nevertheless involves costs, even though, he admitted, it is not clear how much these bonds would cost the number one Swiss bank. The bank had strongly opposed the original government proposal.
In concrete terms, the difference between the Federal Council's April proposal and the CET-S variant is not marginal. The Federal Council was asking that systemically important banks — today, in fact, only UBS would be affected — fully finance their foreign subsidiaries with Common Equity Tier 1 capital (CET-1). CET-S instead proposes that half of the coverage be met through AT1 bonds, a capital instrument that nevertheless has varying degrees of subordination and conversion risk depending on the issuing terms.
### Comparison between the regimes: from 60% to the mixed scenario
To grasp the scope of the change, it may be useful to compare the regimes side by side.
| Regime | Required coverage for foreign participations | Main instrument | |---|---|---| | Current (in force) | 60% | Own capital (composition not detailed in the source) | | Federal Council proposal (April) | 100% | CET-1 only (Common Equity Tier 1 funds) | | CET-S proposal | To be defined in the texts | CET-1 + AT1 bonds (up to about 50%) |
The shift from a 60% regime to a scenario involving AT1 bonds directly affects the liability structure of Swiss systemically important banks, because AT1 bonds are subordinated securities that pay higher coupons than ordinary capital but offer, in return, the possibility of conversion into shares or write-down in the event of a crisis. For outside observers, this means that a larger share of the financing of foreign branches will be absorbed by bond investors rather than by shareholders.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### What changes in practice: possible scenarios
The CET-S text is not yet law: it is a Commission decision that must now go through the parliamentary process. The Commission itself stated that it did not have time to examine the Public Liquidity Backstop mechanism, pointing out that the dossier is still open.
Based on the factual data contained in the source, a few explicit scenarios can be hypothesized, presented as such and not as certain predictions:
Scenario A — A fully compliant systemic bank. A bank that meets all capital requirements can continue to pay dividends, repurchase its own shares, and award bonuses to executives without restrictions. No automatic obligation to issue additional AT1.
Scenario B — A bank falling below requirements. The obligation to suspend dividends and share buybacks kicks in; executive bonuses are reduced or, in the most serious cases, eliminated. The duration and extent of the reduction depend on how long and to what extent the requirements are not met.
Scenario C — Issuing AT1 while in difficulty. The CET-S explicitly provides measures to prevent a bank from issuing AT1 bonds when it is already in a precarious financial situation: in other words, the instrument designed to strengthen capital cannot be used as a last resort.
### How to follow the evolution of the dossier
For those who live or work in Switzerland and want to follow the legislative process of the bank law revision, the operational steps are the following, based exclusively on the information contained in the source:
- Consult the CET-S Council of States press releases to know the text that the Commission will propose to the upper Chamber. - Check the subsequent developments of the dossier, in particular the examination of the Public Liquidity Backstop, which the Commission declared it has not yet had time to examine. - Follow the process in the Council of States and, subsequently, the procedure to eliminate divergences with the National Council, as well as the final stage at the Federal Council.
The concrete impact for Swiss taxpayers, as Ettlin stressed, is the stated objective of "strengthening the rules to better protect taxpayers": the CET-S decision moves in this direction, through a compromise that combines "hard" own funds (CET-1) and hybrid instruments (AT1) with automatic mechanisms suspending dividends and bonuses in case of breach of capital requirements. The final decision now lies with the Council of States.

item.title: Zurich bans headscarves and cell phones in schools
item.description: The Zurich Grand Council approves the ban on headscarves and mobile phones by a narrow margin. Aargau had already decided on the veil. Times: two years for laws.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Zurich approves veil and mobile phone ban at school with narrow votes (87-82, 92-82) - Aargau had already approved veil ban a week earlier (78-54) - Zurich government has 2 years to develop laws compliant with Constitution
## Key facts - **What**: Ban on wearing veils in public schools/kindergartens for girls and women; ban on mobile phones in mandatory education - When: Approvals today by Zurich Grand Council; Aargau a week earlier - Where: Canton Zurich and Canton Aargau - Who: UDC (veil motion), UDC + UDF (mobile phone postulate), State Councils - Votes: 87 in favor-82 against-6 abstentions (veil); 92 in favor-82 against-2 abstentions (mobile phones)
The Zurich Grand Council approved today, with a narrow margin of 87 votes against 82 and six abstentions, a controversial motion by the Union of the Center that calls for a ban on wearing veils for girls and women in all public schools and kindergartens in the canton. Before the parliamentary debate, the Zurich State Council had already indicated its readiness to accept the motion and to draw up legislation compliant with the Constitution. The government now has two years to submit to Parliament a report and a legislative proposal.
The decision comes a week after the Aargau Grand Council had already accepted a similar motion, with 78 votes in favor and 54 against, tasking the cantonal government with drawing up a ban for female students of mandatory education up to the age of 16. In Aargau, however, the State Council had opposed it, arguing that legal obstacles exist, constitutional reservations and issues related to the jurisprudence of the Federal Court.
In the same session today, the Zurich Grand Council approved a second measure: with 92 votes in favor, 82 against and two abstentions, a postulate by the UDC and the Union of Democratic Forces passed, which calls for an absolute ban on mobile phones in mandatory education. The State Council will have to assess the adoption of binding guidelines at cantonal level, also with a two-year deadline to draw up a report.
### Current situation: variety among municipalities
So far, individual Zurich municipalities have addressed the issue of digital devices in [kindergartens](nav:nursery) and school institutions in very different ways, leaving room for fragmented local decisions. The mobile phone ban, as provided for in the approved postulate, would concern smartphones, tablets and notebooks at all levels, from kindergarten to the end of ninth grade. Crucial: the ban would not only apply during lessons, but also during breaks and in all day care facilities and support structures of schools and municipalities.
However, the postulate provides for some specific exceptions: the ban does not apply for documented health reasons. Also excluded are devices managed directly by the school and necessary for carrying out the lessons themselves. This means that if a female teacher uses a didactic tablet, or if a teacher uses devices for integrated learning, these remain permitted. ### Cantonal uniformity against local fragmentation
The approval of the two Zurich measures represents a significant change compared to the current fragmented situation. Today each municipality decides independently: some allow phones in breaks, others ban them completely, others still establish limitations for certain age groups. Cantonal legislation will create a uniform standard, eliminating municipal disparities and ensuring consistency throughout Zurich.
As for the veil, the Zurich decision represents a further strengthening compared to the Argovian motion: it is not limited to compulsory schooling until the age of 16, but extends the ban to all girls and women in schools and public kindergartens without specific age restrictions. This means that even high school students would be subject to the ban, a wider scope than in Aargau.

If the cell phone ban were implemented, each Zurich school would need to comply with binding cantonal guidelines. School administrations would have to develop clear procedures for collecting and storing devices during school hours, communicate the new rules to parents and students, and define consequences for non-compliance. Health-related exceptions would require advance medical documentation from parents or guardians.
For the veil ban, if approved after the legislative process, school administrations would need to review internal regulations and communicate the change to affected families and students. Each school will continue to apply its own local policies on cell phones and head coverings. The Zurich State Council must now begin work on drafting two separate reports: one on the veil ban in public schools and kindergartens, one on the cell phone ban in compulsory education. These reports will need to address questions of administrative feasibility, constitutional compliance, implementation costs, and likely consultations with concerned municipalities and school stakeholders.
Once presented to Parliament (within two years), genuine public and parliamentary debates will begin, where amendments could modify the terms of the bans. It is essential to follow official updates to understand how today's approved motions will translate into actual legislation.

From tomorrow, Swiss farmers will be able to draw on national compulsory protein feed stocks to face the supply difficulties that have been putting pressure on the livestock sector for several weeks. This was decided by the delegate to the Economic Supply of the Country (AEP) Roland Pfister, following the announcement last Wednesday. The measure provides for the possibility of withdrawing a maximum of 20% of the total quantity stored, ### Who impacts the measurement and why
The decision primarily affects the Swiss livestock supply chain, which depends to a significant extent on imports of protein feed for dairy cattle, suviatii and poultry. Soybean meal, expressly recalled by the source, is one of the most important components of the animal food ration, in particular for the poultry and dairy sector, widespread both in German Switzerland — among the main production basins are cantons such as Bern, Lucerne, St. Gallen and Thurgau — and in Romanian Switzerland, with Vaud, Freiburg and Neuchâtel among the most involved areas.

Until the announcement last Wednesday, the mandatory stocks remained intact and unavailable on the market: the processing industry and farmers could only count on regular imports, progressively reduced by the decline in water levels of the Rhine and the Danube. The FSO report examines the portion of the pay gap that cannot be traced back to observable structural factors. ## In a nutshell - Third consecutive decrease: -4% in Ticino, -5.5% in Mesolcina and Calanca - An average household (4,500 kWh) saves CHF 53-73 in 2027 - Energy costs fall by 13-16%, grid increases by 3% - Measurement fee: +CHF 0.20/month for smart meters
## Key facts - **What**: SES electricity tariff reduction for the third consecutive year - When: Year 2027 - Where: Ticino, Mesolcina and Calanca (SES area) - Who: Società Elettrica Sopracenerina SA (Locarno office) - Ticino savings: 53 CHF equivalent to about 4% - Mesolcin/Calanca savings: 73 CHF equivalent to 5.5% - Average consumption: 4,500 kilowatt hours per year
The downward trend in tariffs for customers of Società Elettrica Sopracenerina SA continues. In 2027, for the third consecutive year, SES reports a decline in energy bills thanks to a reduction in supply costs and efficient portfolio management.
In the Ticino area of SES, an average domestic economy with an annual consumption of 4,500 kilowatt hours will save 53 francs, equivalent to about 4%. An even more significant reduction concerns the four municipalities of lower Mesolcina and Calanca served by Sopracenerina: here the drop reaches 73 francs, or 5.5%.
### Tariff structure unchanged, but with specific variations
The tariff structure remains stable compared to 2026. The bill continues to be composed of five elements: network use, metering rate, supply of ### Smart meter: adjustment of the metering tariff
The metering tariff, introduced for the first time in 2026, will be adjusted from CHF 6.10 to CHF 6.30 per month — an increase of CHF 0.20 monthly, equivalent to CHF 2.40 annually. This adjustment is linked to the expected costs of accelerating the replacement of traditional meters with intelligent models (smart meters), in compliance with the current federal regulatory framework.
The smart meter represents an investment in transparency and energy efficiency: it allows customers to monitor consumption in real time, promoting conscious energy use and facilitating the integration of local renewable sources. The installation and management of these devices involve costs that SES gradually transfers to the bill.
For most customers, the CHF 2.40 annual increase is fully offset by the reduction on the energy supply. In fact, the balance is largely positive: the net savings remain at CHF 53 in Ticino or CHF 73 in Mesolcina and Calanca.
### The decisive drop: energy supply
The component that really makes the difference is the energy supply. Compared to 2026, the cost of this item will decrease by approximately 13% for SES customers in Ticino and by about 16% for customers in Graubünden. This drop is significant: while 3% increases on the grid and the smart meter adjustment absorb part of the savings, the energy reduction represents the largest net gain.
SES attributes this result to two strategic factors: the procurement strategy made it possible to minimize the volatility of energy prices over recent months; the well-balanced portfolio of Sopracenerina, characterized by a mix of locally produced renewable energy and energy purchased on the wholesale market.
In practice, thanks to careful management and diversification between local sources and the market, SES has transferred to customers the advantage of lower energy prices in 2027. This approach protected customers from global energy volatility, avoiding steeper increases.

In the context of the [cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living), energy represents a significant item in the family budget. A reduction of CHF 53-73 per year is not marginal: for an average family with standard consumption, it equates to a discount of about 4-5.5% on overall energy spending. ## In a nutshell - In 2025 the PS raised 7.9 million francs, the highest among federal parties - Nine parties declare a total of 24.6 million, down by 1 million compared to 2024 - Mandatory transparency for parties represented in the Federal Assembly
## Key facts - **What**: Revenue declared by Swiss federal parties in 2025 - When: Data published by the Federal Financial Control in 2025 - Where: Swiss Federal Assembly - Who: Federal Financial Control (FFC) - Most Revenue Party: PS with CHF 7.9 million - Total declared: 24.6 million francs (9 parties) - Change: -1 million compared to 2024
## # Political Funding Numbers
The Federal Financial Controller has made public the data on the revenue declared by nine of the ten parties represented in the Federal Assembly for the year 2025. Altogether, the amounts amount to 24.6 million francs, a figure that marks a contraction of about one million compared to the 25.6 million declared in 2024. Leading the national ranking is the Socialist Party (PS) with 7.9 million francs, confirming the party with the highest income ever.
Behind the PS are the Radical Liberal Party (PLR) with 4.8 million, the Centre Democratic Union (UDC) with 3.8 million and the Centre with 2.7 million. The Greens declared 1.8 million francs, while the Liberal Greens stand at 1.2 million. The Remaining Parties — Democratic Union ### What emerges from the data
The overall contraction of one million francs between 2024 and 2025 deserves attention. If the SP maintained absolute leadership, its loss of 0.3 million suggests a slight erosion in fundraising capacity. More relevant is the decline in the PLR, which lost as much as 1.8 million: the figure represents almost 27 percent of the radical party's overall revenue, signaling a significant reduction in its funding base.
Otherwise, the UDC has been able to increase its revenues by 1.0 million francs, a result that positions it as one of the few winners of this round. The Centre, despite having earned only 0.1 million, has at least confirmed a stability in its cash flows. Among the smaller parties, the situation remains more contained. The Greens, with 1.8 million, remain the third pole after PS and PLR for declared revenue volumes, while the liberal Greens are significantly different with 1.2 million.
The lack of data related to the Ticinese League complicates the national picture: not knowing how much this formation has collected prevents having a complete picture of federal political funding in 2025.
### What counts as "revenue"
Importantly, the figures released by the Federal Financial Control do not include all cash flows to parties. Mandatory declarations relate to income from donations, events, sales
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### Transparency and access to data
In Switzerland, the obligation to be transparent about party funding is one of the pillars of federal democracy. Parties that have representation in the Federal Assembly must submit their entry data to public scrutiny every year, according to the rules on the transparency of policy funding. This mechanism allows citizens and researchers to verify the economic sources of the main national political actors.
The Federal Financial Control acts as the body responsible for the collection, verification and publication of this data. The annual reports make the totality of declared revenues public, allowing a cross-cutting view of how parties finance themselves. item.title: Apprenticeship in Graubünden: dual path, AFC and CFC
item.description: Apprenticeship in Graubünden: dual school-company system regulated by the LFPr, AFC and CFC qualifications, salary and professional maturity to access the SUPPL.
item.content:encoded:
## At a glance - Apprenticeship in Switzerland: dual pathway (school + company) regulated at the federal level - Vocational education and training in Graubünden: coordinated offer by the Canton and the Confederation - Vocational baccalaureate: pathway following the apprenticeship for access to universities of applied sciences (FACH) - Apprentice remuneration: set by the Canton/Vocational Education Office, differs by year and sector
## Key facts - **What**: Apprenticeship and vocational education in the Canton of Graubünden - When: current training year (exact dates not specified in the source) - Where: Canton of Graubünden, with reference to the Swiss national framework - Who: Cantonal Office for Vocational Education and Training of Graubünden (name not specified in the source) - How: dual school-company pathway under the VPETA (Federal Act on Vocational Education and Training) - Final qualification: AFC (Federal Certificate of Competence) or CFC (Federal Diploma of VET), depending on duration - Vocational baccalaureate: accessible after the apprenticeship to continue at a university of applied sciences (FACH)
Vocational education and training is the most common post-compulsory pathway in Switzerland, and in the Canton of Graubünden it operates under the same federal legal bases that govern the rest of the country. The VPETA and its related ordinance set the qualifications that can be awarded, the standard durations, and the relationship between vocational school and host company. In the Canton of Graubünden, implementation is the responsibility of the Cantonal Office for Vocational Education and Training, which coordinates the supply of apprenticeship places, vocational schools and federal examinations.
An apprenticeship is run in dual form: three or four days a week in the company and one or two days at vocational school, plus inter-company courses. The source indicates as final qualifications the AFC (attestato federale di capacità) issued after a two-year pathway (abbreviated training, more practice-oriented), and the CFC (certificato federale di capacità) issued after three or four years (more in-depth training with a solid theoretical foundation). Those who obtain an AFC can progress towards an abbreviated CFC, in accordance with cantonal equivalence rules.
### Where to find an apprenticeship in Graubünden The search for an apprenticeship goes through the usual channels of the Swiss system: the national professions portal (orientamento.ch), the regional placement offices (URC) active in Graubünden, the cantonal platforms managed by the Office for Vocational Education and Training, and the direct channels of host companies. Applications are generally submitted with standard dossiers (CV, cover letter, latest school report and summer work certificates). For available positions in Graubünden, [consult the active job listings](nav:jobs). The Swiss dual system offers concrete advantages for both young people and training companies. From the trainee's perspective, the apprenticeship allows earning an income during training, gaining real work experience, and obtaining a federally recognised qualification valued in the labour market. From the companies' perspective, it represents a structured recruitment channel, with contribution relief and the ability to train personnel according to their own needs. In Graubünden, where the economic fabric is characterised by small and medium-sized enterprises in the tourism, construction, crafts, and public services sectors, the apprenticeship remains one of the main gateways into the working world.
On the economic side, the apprentice's salary is set according to cantonal recommendations, which in Graubünden are published by the Cantonal Office for Vocational Education and Training and vary by apprenticeship year and sector. The remuneration takes into account the fact that the trainee already produces part of the added value within the company while continuing their school education in parallel. The salary deductions applied follow federal rules: OASI/DI/IC 5.3% borne by the employee (10.6% total with employer), unemployment insurance 1.1% up to the annual ceiling, and LAA/UVLA between 0.7% and 1.5% depending on the sector of activity. These contributions are not optional and also apply to apprentices hired under an apprenticeship contract.
### Federal vocational maturity and subsequent pathways After obtaining the CFC (Federal Certificate of Competence), it is possible to access the federal vocational maturity, a qualification that opens the doors to the Universities of Applied Sciences (UAS/UAS). In Graubünden, preparation for the federal vocational maturity is offered by the cantonal vocational schools, often in the form of a course parallel to the third or fourth year of apprenticeship (integrated model) or as an additional year after the diploma (post-CFC model). This option is particularly relevant for those who intend to continue their studies without going through a liceo/gymnasium.
An often overlooked aspect concerns the trainee's insurance cover during the apprenticeship: as an employee, they are insured against occupational and non-occupational accidents through the employer (UVL/LAA) and, as a resident, are required to take out health insurance under the LAMal within three months of arrival in Switzerland (or of starting work) — an aspect that may concern cross-border apprentices or those coming from other cantons.
In terms of contractual rights, the apprentice benefits from the federal labour legislation applicable in all cantons: a maximum weekly working time of 45 hours in industry/office/sales sectors and 50 hours in other sectors, minimum holiday of four weeks (five for those under 20), and protection against abusive dismissal under the Code of Obligations. There is no federal minimum wage, and in Graubünden no cantonal minimum wage is currently in force.
From a tax perspective, apprentices with their own income are subject to federal direct tax (IFD), cantonal tax, and municipal tax, according to the three-level system in force throughout Switzerland. To fill in the tax return, [use the tax return guide](nav:tax-return). To simulate the impact of gross/net salary, [open the salary calculator](nav:calculator).
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). Obtaining an apprenticeship position in Graubünden requires a structured process. Here are the concrete steps to follow, based on the standard procedures of the Swiss vocational training system.
### Step-by-step application procedure 1. Identify the desired profession by consulting the national professions catalogue at orientamento.ch. 2. Prepare an updated CV, a personalised cover letter, and gather your last two school reports. 3. Check the listings published on the Graubünden cantonal portal and contact companies in the field directly. 4. Attend selection interviews bringing, if possible, certificates of internships or summer work experience. 5. Once you have secured a position, sign the apprenticeship contract: the document involves three parties (apprentice, company, and Canton) and specifies the profession, duration, schedule, remuneration, and the rights and duties of the parties. 6. Enrol at the relevant vocational school through the Graubünden Cantonal Office for Vocational Education and Training.
### Deadlines and useful documents Applications for the following training year are typically concentrated between September and February of the preceding year. The Canton publishes annual salary recommendations for apprentices, broken down by apprenticeship year and sector. For updated figures, it is necessary to consult directly the website of the Graubünden Cantonal Office for Vocational Education and Training, as the precise amounts vary from year to year.
For those coming from abroad, it is advisable to also check the permit regime: a non-EU/EFTA foreign apprentice requires a B residence permit issued by the SEM (State Secretariat for Migration), tied to the signing of the apprenticeship contract.
### Useful tools for the reader For those looking for a related job after the apprenticeship, [consult the active job listings](nav:jobs) and [the companies hiring](nav:companies) on the portal. To assess your future salary or the tax impact of apprentice income, [use the salary calculator](nav:calculator). To learn more about mandatory health insurance coverage, [consult the LAMal guide](nav:health).

## In a nutshell - Real estate purchase in Switzerland: 6-12 months from research to transcription - Minimum own funds: usually 20% of the purchase price - Acquisition tax and notary fees vary by canton and municipality - Mortgage mortgage sustainability assessed on income capacity
## Key facts - **What**: Residential purchase in Switzerland - When: Process 6-12 months - Where: Canton of Graubünden - Who: Buyer, bank, notary, cantonal land registers - Regulations: Federal Bond Code - Cost base: Mortgage + acquisition taxes + notary fees + transcription
### The real estate buying process in Switzerland
The purchase of a house in Switzerland follows a process governed by the Federal Bond Code, with cantonal variations on taxation and procedures. The Canton of Graubünden, like all cantons, applies its own rates on acquisition taxes and regulates notarial expenses according to cantonal tariffs.
The main phases are: property search, price negotiation, bank pre-qualification to verify the sustainability of the loan, stipulation of the notarial contract (mandatory), and transcription in the cantonal land registers. Each stage involves specific legal costs and responsibilities.
### Who leads the process: bank, notary and registers
The Swiss bank evaluates the sustainability of the mortgage loan on the basis of the buyer's income capacity, applying a stress-test that simulates scenarios of rising ### Mortgage financing: own funds and sustainability
Access to the mortgage loan in Switzerland requires own funds (usually 20% of the purchase price) and borrowing capacity (sufficient income for mortgage installments and other charges). A lower own fund percentage is possible at some banks, but it comes with a premium mortgage and significant additional costs.
Swiss banks assess the borrowing capacity on the buyer's gross income, deducting [assicurazione malattia obbligatoria (LAMal/KVG)](nav:health), [contributi previdenziali AVS/LPP](nav:pension), federal/cantonal/municipal taxes and other charges. They also apply a stress-test, simulating a high interest rate (usually +1-2%) to verify the sustainability of the mortgage in the scenario of rising rates decided by the Swiss National Bank (SNB). This conservative approach aims to avoid over-indebtedness of buyers.
### Fixed and variable rates
The loan can be variable rate (linked to market rates and the SNB's monetary policy) or fixed (contracted for 3, 5, 10+ years). Floating rates are more flexible but expose you to upside risk; fixed rates offer certainty but usually at higher initial premiums. ## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### The step-by-step purchase procedure
1. **Search and negotiation** (1-6 months): Identify the property, verify its legal situation, and negotiate the price.
2. Bank pre-qualification (1-3 weeks): Contact the bank with income documentation to obtain a pre-qualification letter, which confirms the maximum mortgage accessible.
3. Notarial contract (1-3 weeks): The notary drafts the sale contract, verifies the property's legal situation (absence of liens, encumbrances, easements), and obtains the parties' signatures.

Notary fees are defined by cantonal tariffs and proportional to the purchase price. These also vary from canton to canton. Request quotes from the notary before signing.

item.title: Apprenticeship and vocational training in Graubünden: a complete guide
item.description: Dual school-company model in the Graubünden: internship contract, salary per year, professional maturity and living costs for the apprentice.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Vocational training in Graubünden: dual path school + company - Internship contract governing duration, hours and remuneration - Professional maturity obtainable in parallel with the internship - Apprentice salary varies by training year and sector
## Key facts - **What**: Apprenticeship and vocational training in the Canton of Graubünden - Where: Canton of Graubünden (Switzerland), under the supervision of the Cantonal Office for Vocational Training - Who: Canton of Graubünden, Swiss Confederation, training companies, vocational schools - How: dual system (company + vocational school) regulated by the Federal Law on Vocational Training (LFPr) - Final title: federal certificate of ability (AFC) or federal certificate of practical training (CFP)
Vocational training in Switzerland is regulated at the federal level by the Law on Vocational Training (LFPr), which defines its principles, and finds concrete application in each Canton, including Graubünden. The Swiss system is based on the so-called "dual model": the apprentice carries out practical training in a company and theoretical training in a vocational school at the same time, with intercompany courses that complete the path.
### The internship contract
The internship contract is the document that governs the relationship between the apprentice (or his/her representative, if a minor) and the training company. Before the entry into force of the ### Professional maturity: an additional opportunity
Professional maturity (MP) is a secondary qualification II that is obtained in parallel with the internship. It is divided into seven areas (health, social, visual and applied arts, economics, technique, architecture and natural sciences) and is open to holders of a federal certificate of ability or, in some cases, during the last year of the internship for candidates who meet the school requirements.
Obtaining the MP allows access, without further examination, to professional university schools (SUPs) in the respective subject area. To enroll in a university (ETH or cantonal university), on the other hand, gymnasial maturity or the passing of a complementary exam is required.
### Apprentice living costs and conditions
The cost of living in Switzerland is high and has a real impact on an apprentice's monthly budget. Accommodation is one of the main items, regulated by federal law (art. 253 et seq. CO) the same in each canton. The security deposit can be a maximum of three months' rent, it must be paid into a restricted account in the tenant's name. The cancellation of the landlord requires the official cantonal form, and the tenant can dispute it within thirty days to the conciliation authority.
Health insurance (LAMal) is mandatory for anyone residing in Switzerland. People moving for internship must take out coverage within three months
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Concrete procedure: how to proceed step by step
Finding an apprenticeship position in the Canton of Graubünden requires following a reasoned sequence of steps, which should ideally be started well in advance of the beginning of the apprenticeship.
The first step is to identify the desired sector and profession, by consulting the professional profiles published by the Federal Office for Professional Education and Technology (UFFT/BFTB). For each profession, the description of the skills, the duration of the training, and the list of schools involved are available.
The second step consists of preparing a complete application, made up of a cover letter, an updated CV, copies of school certificates and, where available, internship certificates or references. The cover letter should be tailored to the company and the chosen profession. In the most sought-after sectors, it is useful to apply to several companies, both directly and through job placement portals.
The third step is attending an exploratory interview, during which the company assesses the candidate's aptitudes and the candidate evaluates the work environment. Once the interview is passed, the parties sign an apprenticeship contract drawn up in writing and compliant with cantonal law.
The fourth step is the registration of the contract with the cantonal office for professional education in Graubünden, which verifies its compliance and enrolls the apprentice in the school pathway. The office also provides information on the planned inter-company courses.
### Deadlines and key moments
Applications for apprenticeship positions are concentrated in the autumn of the year preceding the start of the training. Companies publish vacancies starting from late summer and conduct interviews during the autumn months. Enrolments for the school subjects at the vocational school generally take place by the end of the year.
For holders of a B or C permit, the right of access to an apprenticeship is equal to that of Swiss citizens, subject to sectoral exceptions. For holders of a G permit, employment in Switzerland is linked to the cross-border employment relationship, and an apprenticeship is only possible if the job is carried out mainly in the canton's area of work.
### Useful tools and practical information
For those approaching vocational education and training in Switzerland, it is useful to consult the Confederation's berufsberatung.ch portal, which offers career guidance tests and detailed descriptions of the professions. In parallel, the orientamento.ch portal allows you to compare the access requirements for the different professions.
To estimate an apprentice's monthly budget (net salary, social contributions, accommodation, health insurance premiums) it is useful to use a dedicated calculator that takes into account the 5.3% AVS/AI/IPG deduction borne by the employee and the 1.1% for unemployment insurance, within the annual cap set by law. For LAMal premiums, the cantons publish each year the average premiums by region, useful as a starting reference.
Calculate your net salary in Switzerland with our [salary calculator](nav:calculator) and check in advance how much the apprentice will take home, taking into account taxes, contributions and health insurance premiums. The first step is gathering the worker's documents (valid passport, CV, training certificates, signed employment contract) and providing a detailed description of the intended position. This is followed by a check with the competent cantonal labor market offices, aimed at ascertaining the priority of workers already registered as unemployed or residing in Switzerland. The file is then processed by the cantonal migration office, which issues the L permit after notification or SEM approval depending on the applicant's nationality.
### What to do in case of renewal or change of employer
If the employment ends before the permit expires, the holder is required to report it to the cantonal office; a change of employer, even within the same canton, requires a new application, with a reassessment of the case. Extension beyond twelve months is allowed only in exceptional circumstances provided for by federal law, such as the continuation of an assignment for documented reasons not attributable to the will of the worker or the employer.

item.title: Residence permit C Graubünden: requirements and application
item.description: The C permit is the permanent residence permit in Switzerland. Find out how to apply in the canton of Graubünden, the years of residence required, the tax implications, AVS/LPP and the path to ordinary naturalisation.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Permit C: permanent residence in Switzerland after 10 years (5 for EU/EFTA) - Managed by cantonal office Graubünden + Federal Secretariat of State for Migration (SEM) - It does not expire, unlike the B permit renewable every 5 years - Paves the way for ordinary naturalization after 10 years of full residency
## Key facts - **What**: Residence permit C — Swiss permanent residence license - Who: Issued by Canton Grisons + Federal Secretariat of State for Migration (SEM) - Requirements: 10 years ordinary residence in Switzerland; 5 years for EU/EFTA citizens - Naturalization: Permit C + 10 years total residence + cantonal/municipal requirements - Implications: Federal-cantonal-communal taxation; AVS/AI/LPP contributions; mandatory LAMal coverage
Residence permit C is the permanent residence permit in Switzerland, issued by the canton with validation by the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) at the federal level. It represents the third level in permits for resident foreigners: after the L permit (short duration, up to 1 year) and the B permit (residence, renewable on a periodic basis).
Anyone who ordinarily resides in Switzerland for a minimum of 10 consecutive years can apply for the C permit. For citizens of the European Union and the European Free Trade Association (EU/EFTA), the term is reduced to 5 years. In the canton of Graubünden, as in every canton, the request is submitted to the competent cantonal office, the The C permit transforms the tax and social security position of the resident foreigner. First of all, with the C permit you become ** ordinary resident ** in Switzerland for federal, cantonal and municipal tax purposes. The Swiss tax calculator estimates the federal-cantonal taxation accurately based on the declared income.
### Federal, cantonal and municipal taxation
Direct Federal Tax (DFI) applies to the resident's worldwide income. The cantonal and municipal taxes of the canton of Graubünden follow the rates and multipliers of each municipality (the municipal multiplier applies to the cantonal tax base). Deductions may relate to AVS/AI/LPP contributions and payments to the third pillar 3a, subject to indexed annual ceilings. Each canton and municipality disseminates public tax tables: the canton of Graubünden publishes rates and multipliers for each municipality on the official website.
### Mandatory social security contributions
With the C permit, the resident is required to pay contributions towards the three pillars of social security. AVS/AI/IPG requires 5.3% to be paid by the employee (10.6% total with employer). The LPP (compulsory occupational pension from first employment) applies rates by age group: 7% for 25–34 years, 10% for 35–44, 15% for 45–54, 18% for 55+ up to the reference age. The [comparatore pensioni](nav:pension) helps to estimate future rent.
### Mandatory sickness coverage
Sickness coverage (LAMal/KVG) becomes mandatory within 3 months
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## How to apply for permit C in the Canton of Grisons
The process is managed at two levels: cantonal and federal. The canton is the first point of contact; the SEM validates at the national level.
### Phase 1: Document preparation
Before submitting your application, gather: - A valid passport or identity document - A residence certificate from the municipality of current domicile in Switzerland - An extract from the Swiss criminal register (requestable online or at the cantonal police) - Proof of financial stability (employment contract, AVS contribution payments, recent pay slips) - Any cantonal integration certificates (if required by the Canton of Grisons)
The Canton of Grisons specifies the exact list on the migration office website. Some requirements are canton-specific; contact them directly for current details.
### Phase 2: Submission at the Grisons cantonal office
Check the address and opening hours of the migration office (Kantonales Amt für Migration). The application is submitted in person or by registered mail to the office, together with the attachments. Not all cantons accept online applications — check directly before making the trip.
### Phase 3: Transmission to SEM and federal decision
The cantonal office verifies the completeness of the application. If everything is correct, it forwards the file to the SEM (State Secretariat for Migration, based in Bern, Permits Section). The SEM conducts a federal check: criminal record, international data, compliance with migration rules. The decision is sent to the canton, which notifies the applicant of the outcome. Times: on average 2–6 months from submission, depending on cantonal and federal workload.
### Phase 4: Collection and municipal registration
Once approved, permit C is handed over at the cantonal office. It must be registered with the municipality of residence within the indicated deadlines. Registration activates tax and social security rights.
## The path to ordinary naturalisation
Holders of permit C have an open door to ordinary Swiss naturalisation. The federal requirements are: already holding permit C, 10 years of total residence in Switzerland (the last 5 years with permit C count double, therefore reducing the minimum to 5 years with C), no serious criminal record in the last 5 years. In addition, specific municipal and cantonal requirements apply (these vary: some municipalities require knowledge of a national language, additional integration criteria, respect for the cantonal constitution).
The naturalisation application is submitted in two phases: first to the Canton of Grisons, then to the municipality of residence. Each authority has its own deadlines, administrative fees (generally CHF 100–300) and approval procedures.
## Next steps
Use the [Swiss payslip calculator](nav:calculator) to estimate your monthly net pay with federal-cantonal deductions once you have permit C. Check the official Canton of Grisons website for application forms and migration office contact details. If you have children, consider family allowances and cantonal income support benefits. Consult a tax advisor to plan the transition from cross-border worker (if applicable) to ordinary resident, given the significant variation in taxation.

item.title: Naturalization Canton Zug: requirements and complete procedure
item.description: Permit C, 10 years of residence (ages 8-18 count double) and ITER at three levels: municipal, cantonal and federal. Here's how it works in Zug.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Ordinary naturalization in Switzerland requires C permit and 10 years of residence - In the Canton of Zug, specific cantonal and municipal requirements are added - The years of residence between 8 and 18 years old count twice for the purposes of the period - The procedure includes language tests, integration tests and the payment of taxes
## Key facts - **What**: Requirements and procedure for ordinary naturalization in the Canton of Zug - Who: Foreign citizens with residence permit (C) residing in the Canton - Where: Canton of Zug, Switzerland - Federal legal basis: Swiss Citizenship Act (LStr) and related ordinance - Minimum residence: 10 years in Switzerland, with ages between 8 and 18 counting double - Permit required: Permit C (domicile), issued normally after 10 years of residence (5 for EU/EFTA citizens) - Taxation levels: 3 levels (federal + cantonal + municipal DFI), with their own multipliers for each Canton and Municipality
Ordinary naturalisation in the Canton of Zug follows a two-tier process: a federal level, governed by the Swiss Citizenship Act, and a cantonal-communal level, with specific rules of the Canton and the Municipality of residence. To apply you must hold a C permit — the residence permit, which is usually issued in Switzerland after 10 years of residence (5 years for EU or EFTA nationals) — and have at least 10 years of residence in Switzerland. In this The naturalization procedure in the Canton of Zug differs from that of other Cantons due to the bureaucratic speed and clarity of the requirements, elements that also derive from the small size of the Canton. Understanding the practical implications of this process means knowing where the three levels of competence — federal, cantonal and municipal — are located and how they interact.
### Economic and tax implications for the future citizen
Obtaining a Swiss passport brings practical benefits that go beyond the right to vote. From a fiscal point of view, the naturalized citizen is subject to the same IFD + cantonal + municipal regime as any other resident. In Switzerland there is no federal minimum wage (while some cantons — not Zug among those with a mandatory cantonal minimum wage — have their own). The new citizen of Zug will enter a labor market that, for working hours, refers to federal law: maximum 45 hours per week in industry, offices and sales, 50 hours in other sectors; at least 4 weeks of vacation (5 under the age of 20).
On the pension front, naturalisation does not change either the AVS/AHV position or the LPP/BVG situation. The AVS/AI/IPG contributions amount to 5.3% borne by the employee (10.6% total with the employer), AD/AC to 1.1% up to the annual ceiling, LAINF/LAA between 0.7% and 1.5% depending on the sector. LPP/BVG predicts increasing contributions with age
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). Obtaining Swiss citizenship in the Canton of Zug requires a structured process, with precise steps to follow and documents to prepare. The procedure is well-known for being well organized, but it remains articulated across three distinct levels.
### Step-by-step procedure
**1. Check of prerequisites.** First of all, you must ensure that you hold a C permit and have completed at least 10 years of residence in Switzerland (years between age 8 and 18 count double). For EU/EFTA citizens, the C permit can be issued after 5 years of residence according to SEM rules.
2. Document collection. You will need: a valid identity document, C permit, proof of residence, language certificate (German for Zug, at the level required by cantonal law), extract from the Swiss criminal record, certificate of absence of debts (Debt Collection and Bankruptcy Office), proof of financial self-sufficiency, birth certificate and, where applicable, marriage certificate or documents relating to minor children.
3. Municipal application. The first application is submitted to the municipality of residence. Each municipality in the Canton of Zug sets its own additional requirements (years of municipal residence, knowledge of local realities) and its own fee. The municipal council (Gemeinderat) and, in many cases, the municipal assembly (Gemeindeversammlung) or the electorate vote on the granting.
4. Cantonal application. After municipal approval, the application is forwarded to the Migration and Citizenship Office of the Canton of Zug, which verifies cantonal requirements (residence in the canton, integration test, German language, knowledge of cantonal realities). The cantonal fee is paid.
5. Federal application. Once municipal and cantonal approvals have been obtained, the file is forwarded to Bern for the issuance of the federal naturalization authorization. The Confederation checks for the absence of grounds for revocation (serious convictions, dependence on social assistance, etc.) and issues the federal naturalization act.
6. Ceremony and acquisition of Swiss citizenship. Once the process is complete, the applicant obtains the Swiss passport and is registered in the civil status register.
### Where to go and useful tools
For up-to-date information on the specific requirements of the Canton of Zug and your municipality of residence, it is advisable to consult directly the Canton's website (Zuger Verwaltung) and that of the municipality. At the federal level, the reference is SEM (State Secretariat for Migration), which publishes guides and forms. Naturalization fees — federal, cantonal, and municipal — vary in exact amount: it is recommended to request them directly from the relevant offices before starting the procedure.
For those who are dealing with their salary in Switzerland and want to understand the tax impact of their situation — also in view of a change of status — the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) by Frontaliere Ticino is available, useful for simulating net pay and AVS/LPP pension contributions based on the Canton of work.
To get an overview of the overall cost of living in Switzerland — rents, health insurance premiums, taxes — the guide to the [cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) offers an updated general picture.
If the goal is to better understand the Swiss tax system before tackling naturalization, the page dedicated to the [tax return](nav:tax-return) can also be a good starting point.

item.title: LAMal Canton Grisons Awards: deductibles and reduction
item.description: Guide to health insurance premiums in the Canton of Graubünden: deductibles from CHF 300 to 2500, alternative models, reduction subsidies and application procedure.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - KVG: compulsory health insurance for Swiss residents - Adult deductibles range from CHF 300 to CHF 2500 (choice of contractor) - Each canton administers premiums and subsidies for reduction
## Key Facts - What: Private health insurance at per capita premiums, not tax - When: Mandatory for residents, stipulated within 3 months of arrival - Where: Single system in all Swiss cantons (including Graubünden) - Who: FSIO/BSV coordinates at federal level; cantons set premiums and subsidies - Amount: Deductibles from CHF 300 (minimum) to CHF 2500 (maximum) for adults
In the canton of Graubünden, as in every Swiss canton, compulsory health insurance (KVG or KVG in German) represents a structural cost for residents. The KVG is not a tax but a private insurance with per capita premiums: each person takes out a free choice of insurer. Premiums vary according to age group, canton (and sometimes region within the canton) and insurance model chosen.
At federal level, FSIO/BSV (Federal Social Insurance Office) coordinates the overall system. However, the cantons independently determine the premiums charged by companies operating in their territory and determine the requirements and amount of subsidies for premium reductions for residents with low incomes.
### Standardised deductibles and cover models
The KVG provides federally standardised deductibles for adults: CHF 300, CHF 500, CHF 1000, CHF 1500, CHF 2000 and CHF 2500. The deductible is the first amount that the insured person incurs out of pocket when seeking outpatient treatment, before the insurance company starts covering the costs. Choosing a higher deductible means paying lower monthly premiums, but taking on more risks in the event of many treatments. Conversely, a low deductible (CHF 300) means higher premiums, but protects against significant unexpected outlays.
In the canton of Graubünden, as in the rest of Switzerland, each insured person evaluates the compromise between monthly premium and protection according to his or her health needs and financial capacity. [Scopri le opzioni di copertura della tua LAMal](nav:health) and compare the available deductibles. ### Alternative insurance models in Graubünden
In addition to the choice of deductible, LAMal offers alternative insurance models that allow the premium to be reduced in exchange for limitations on access to benefits. Among these is the model with a mandatory general practitioner: the contractor enrolls with a trusted doctor and addresses the diagnostic path under his guidance, except for emergencies and certain specialties (ophthalmology, gynecology). Another model is the limited choice insurance of the hospital (network), where access to hospital facilities is restricted to those agreed with the company.
The Canton of Graubünden has particular geographical characteristics — isolated valleys, a population scattered over a vast territory — that influence the offer of alternative models: not all solutions are available everywhere for reasons of territorial accessibility. Check which models are available in your area of Graubünden.
### Cantonal subsidies and premium reductions
Each Swiss canton financially supports low-income residents through subsidies for the reduction of LAMal premiums. The Canton of Graubünden, like the other cantons, provides cantonal funds and federal contributions to reduce the burden for those who cannot afford full premiums. Access criteria and the amount of the reduction vary from canton to canton, as each canton establishes its own income and assets thresholds.

For premium reduction requests in the Canton of Graubünden, the resident must contact the competent cantonal administration (typically the Office of Public Health or the Office of Social Economy, depending on the local organizational structure). Often the canton provides an online or paper application form on the official website of the regional administration.
The premium reduction request is not automatic: it must be submitted every year according to the deadlines set by the canton itself (usually with a deadline fixed in spring or autumn). Attach income documentation to the application: tax declaration for the two previous years, bank statements, or employer certificate, as required by the cantonal administration.
### Step-by-step to request the premium reduction subsidy
1. Access the website of the Graubünden cantonal administration and look for the section dedicated to LAMal or health insurance subsidies. Note the annual deadline for submitting applications and the current income thresholds. 2. Collect tax documentation: prepare a copy of the cantonal/municipal tax declaration, recent pay slips, unemployment certificate if applicable, bank statements. 3. Fill in the official form, completing every field accurately: residence in Graubünden, number of insured persons in the household, total amount of LAMal premiums paid annually. 4. Submit the request to the indicated office, respecting the annual deadline (in-person delivery, ordinary mail, or registered email). 5. Wait for the notification of the outcome from the administration, which normally verifies the data and communicates the result within a few weeks to two months. 6. If the request is approved, the subsidy is normally paid directly to the insurer, which reduces the insured person's premium accordingly starting from the following month or the following year.
### Annual updates and changes in situation
The premium reduction is not permanent: every year the income situation must be recertified. An increase in income or assets may lead to a reduction or complete loss of the subsidy. Conversely, a decrease in income (for example, switching to part-time or a temporary job loss) could open rights to a greater reduction. It is advisable to check every year whether the conditions have changed and, if necessary, submit a new request. Some cantons allow updating the data during the year if the situation changes significantly.

item.title: Buying Zug house: prices, mortgage and costs
item.description: Complete guide to buying real estate in the Canton of Zug: transfer costs, own funds, mortgage loan and cantonal taxes.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Buying a house in Switzerland requires equity capital and an assessment of mortgage affordability. - The transfer tax and notary fees vary by canton and municipality; the Canton of Zug follows its specific cantonal regulations. - Real estate taxation involves three levels: federal (DIT), cantonal and municipal, with different multipliers for each jurisdiction.
## Key facts - **What**: Property purchase in Switzerland through a federal and cantonal administrative procedure - Tax levels: federal DIT + cantonal + municipal (each canton has its own multipliers) - Competences: FTA/ESTV manages the DIT; cantonal administrations manage local taxes - Essential requirement: Equity capital to access bank mortgages - Actors: Notary, banks, Land Registry, cantonal tax offices - Reference rate: SNB sets the national key rate for mortgages
### Three levels of taxation in the purchase process
Buying a house in Switzerland involves a complex interaction between three administrative levels: federal, cantonal and municipal. The taxation burden on real estate transactions reflects this three-pillar structure. At the federal level, the direct federal tax (DIT) applies, which targets the income and capital of property owners. At the cantonal and municipal level, complementary taxes apply to the transfer of real estate ownership.
In the Canton of Zug, as in every Swiss canton, the transfer tax is governed by specific cantonal laws. The cantonal administration sets rates, exemption thresholds and the collection procedure; municipalities can add their own local multiplier. This means that two property purchases of the same economic value, carried out in different cantons, will generate significantly different tax burdens.
The FTA (Federal Tax Administration) and the ESTV (Conference of Cantonal Finance Directors) coordinate the tax system at the national level, but cantonal laws remain sovereign with regard to local taxes. Those buying a house in the Canton of Zug must therefore consult the cantonal tax office to find out exactly the charge applicable to the transfer of ownership in their municipality.
### Equity capital and mortgage access: affordability assessment
A central aspect of buying property in Switzerland is the availability of equity capital and the financial capacity to service the mortgage over time. Swiss banks require a minimum amount of equity capital — defined by each institution's lending policy — before granting a mortgage for the acquisition of a residential property. Mortgage affordability is assessed on the basis of the buyer's income and their ability to make monthly payments over decades. A [salary calculator](nav:calculator) can help estimate the net disposable income and the capacity to service the mortgage.
This assessment process is national — it follows Swiss banking standards and guidelines issued by the Swiss National Bank (SNB) — even though each bank applies its own selection criteria and interest rate pricing. Those intending to acquire a home in the Canton of Zug must therefore present a solid financial plan to local banks, or to institutions elsewhere in Switzerland, to access financing. ### The role of the notary and transfer fees
The transfer of real estate ownership in Switzerland is governed by federal law (Code of Obligations, CO) and by complementary cantonal regulations. The deed of sale — the public transfer document — must be drafted and signed before a notary, whose task is to verify the identity of the parties, the absence of undeclared mortgage debts, and the formal regularity of the contract. Notary fees are borne by the buyer and vary by canton: each canton has its own notary tariffs set by local legislative decrees.
Alongside notary fees, there are administrative charges related to the transfer of ownership rights at the Land Registry office (municipal/cantonal jurisdiction). These amounts also depend on the value of the property and on local regulations. There is no single federal tariff; each canton defines its own collection procedures.
### Mortgage loan and interest rates
The mortgage loan is the main financing instrument for the purchase of residential properties in Switzerland. Once the property has been identified and the required documentation has been collected (pay slips, bank statements, tax returns), the client negotiates the interest rate and the term of the loan with the bank. The Swiss National Bank (SNB) sets the reference rate (key rate) of Swiss monetary policy; mortgage rates follow correlated movements, but each bank applies its own spread and its own commercial policy.
A hypothetical situation: a buyer who has sufficient own funds and a stable income can negotiate a fixed-rate mortgage for 10–20 years. During this period, the mortgage service — the monthly payment of principal and interest — remains constant. Once the term expires, the borrower will need to renegotiate the mortgage or repay the debt using other sources. Contact the [Swiss banks](nav:banks) in the Canton of Zug or in your area to discuss the available financing options and current rates.
### Before signing: energy assessment and technical survey
Before signing the purchase contract, a prudent buyer requests a technical survey of the property to verify its structural condition, plumbing and electrical systems, and other structural risk factors. Moreover, Switzerland has introduced energy efficiency requirements: every building must declare its energy status according to cantonal regulations (which can vary significantly). These checks are not uniformly imposed by federal law, but they are advisable and sometimes required by banks as a condition for financing. The technical survey protects the buyer from hidden renovation costs and allows for a more realistic assessment of the economic sustainability of the investment.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Step-by-step procedure for purchasing a property
1. **Search and negotiation**: Identify the property through a real estate agent or online portal, and negotiate the price with the seller. This phase has no federal deadlines — it is purely commercial.
2. Bank pre-qualification: Contact one or more banks and request a mortgage pre-qualification. The bank will verify your income, existing debts, and available own funds, and will communicate the maximum amount that can be financed.
3. Purchase offer: Once the price has been agreed upon, the client or the agent drafts a written offer (sometimes it is a purchase promise subject to various conditions, including financing). The offer defines the price, the delivery date, and any suspensive conditions.
4. Verification of ownership at the Land Registry: Before committing, the buyer (through a notary or agent) verifies that the seller is actually the owner and that there are no hidden mortgages or encumbrances. This is a federal duty of diligence and is registered with the cantonal/municipal Land Registry office.
5. Signing of the deed before the notary: Once the financing has been confirmed by the bank and the documents have been verified, the parties go to the notary to sign the transfer deed. The notary draws up the deed, verifies the identity of the contracting parties, confirms the absence of disputes, and signs the deed.
6. Registration in the Land Registry: Within a short period (variable by canton), the notary files the deed with the competent Land Registry office. The registration legally transfers ownership to the new owner.
7. Mortgage disbursement and payment: After registration in the Registry, the bank disburses the mortgage and pays the seller. From this moment, the buyer is the owner and must begin paying the monthly mortgage.
### Practical tools: where to find information and calculate your purchasing capacity
To assess your payment capacity and the sustainability of the mortgage, it is useful to consult online calculation resources. You can also check information on the [cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living) to understand the total impact of the purchase on your overall budget.
Consult the cantonal Land Registry office of Zug for exact notary fees, property transfer tax rates, and the local property registration procedure. Cantonal real estate agencies and notary firms provide up-to-date information on current financing rates and banking conditions.
Finally, it is advisable to consult a notary specialized in real estate law or a cantonal tax advisor to understand exactly what the tax and administrative burdens will be in your specific case.
Start evaluating your financial situation: Use our [calculator](nav:calculator) to estimate your financing capacity and the monthly sustainability of the mortgage based on your available net income.

item.description: How to obtain and renew the residence permit B in the Canton of Zug: documents, duration up to 5 years for EU/EFTA and bureaucratic steps.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Permit B issued by the Cantonal Office of Migration of Zug - Requires employment contract, adequate housing and means of subsistence - Typical duration 5 years for EU/EFTA citizens, renewable on request - Documents and forms available on the cantonal portal
## Key facts - **What**: Residence permit B (Aufenthaltsbewilligung) in the Canton of Zug - When: Issuance and renewal according to the Federal Law on Foreigners (LStrI) - Where: Canton of Zug, German-speaking Switzerland - Who: Cantonal Office for Migration (Amt für Migration) in Zug, under the supervision of the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) - Requirements: Profit-making activity, adequate accommodation, ascertained identity, sufficient financial means - Duration: Up to 5 years for EU/EFTA citizens; duration linked to the employment contract for third-country nationals - Renewal: Early application before the deadline, verification of conditions, cantonal decision - Documents: Passport, employment contract, accommodation certificate, photos, cantonal forms
The B residence permit in Switzerland is the authorization that allows a foreign national to reside in the country for a period of more than one year, with the possibility of renewal. In the Canton of Zug, the issuance and management of this permit is the responsibility of the Cantonal Office for Migration (Amt für Migration), which operates on the basis of the Federal Law on Foreigners and their Integration (LStrI) and in coordination with the Secretariat of Obtaining the B permit in the Canton of Zug means entering an administrative system that combines federal legislation and cantonal practice. The framework conditions are defined by the LStrI and the ALC, but the methods of submitting the application, the required documentation and the processing times are established at the cantonal level. This creates concrete differences between an applicant who goes to the Zug office compared, for example, to those who go to the similar office of another Canton.
### Practical implications for the applicant
The first practical decision is about timing. The B permit is never automatic: even for EU/EFTA citizens, renewal requires the submission of an application for an extension before the expiry of the licence, accompanied by verification of the original conditions (employment, accommodation, integration) and a new decision by the cantonal authority. Sending the application late may result in the interruption of the right of residence and the obligation to leave the country.
The documentation to be produced typically includes the valid passport, a passport format photo, the employment contract or an employer confirmation, the accommodation attestation (rental contract or owner's certificate), and the specific forms provided by the Cantonal Office of Migration. Reunited family members also need certificates of marital status and, if required, documents attesting to the family relationship.

Obtaining or renewing the B permit in the Canton of Zug requires a precise procedure, marked by bureaucratic steps that the applicant can manage independently or with the support of a consultant specialized in immigration law. Below is an operational procedure based on federal and cantonal practice.
### Step-by-step procedure
**Step 1 — Document collection.** The applicant must prepare: a valid passport or identity document, an employment contract (or confirmation from the employer), proof of accommodation in the Canton of Zug, a passport-size photo, and the completed cantonal application forms. For family reunification: translated and, where applicable, legalized civil status certificates.
Step 2 — Submission of the application. The application is submitted to the Cantonal Migration Office of Zug, either directly or through the municipality of residence. Some municipalities act as a first-level desk and forward the documentation to the cantonal office. It is advisable to check on the Canton's website whether the municipality of residence offers this service.
Step 3 — Awaiting the decision. The Cantonal Office verifies compliance with the requirements (employment, accommodation, sufficient financial means, and any relevant absence of criminal record) and issues the B permit. For EU/EFTA citizens with an employment contract, the decision is generally quick; for more complex cases, processing times are longer.
Step 4 — Registration and post-issuance obligations. Once the B permit is obtained, the holder must register with the municipality of residence, take out mandatory health insurance (LAMal) within three months of arrival, and — if starting a gainful activity — register for social contributions (AVS/AI/IPG 5.3% borne by the employee, AD 1.1% up to the maximum, LAINF variable by sector, LPP with increasing rates by age bracket).
Step 5 — Renewal. The B permit is not renewed automatically: before its expiry, the holder must submit a renewal application to the Cantonal Migration Office, demonstrating that the original conditions still apply (employment, adequate accommodation, integration). Practice recommends starting the procedure at least two to three months before the expiry date.
### Useful tools and references
On the Canton of Zug portal, application forms, document checklists, and the contact details of the Cantonal Migration Office are available. For general information on the permit system, the website of the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) can also be consulted.

item.title: Opening a business in Glarus: trade register and costs
item.description: Practical guide to legal forms, registration in the commercial register and tax and insurance obligations for those who start a business in the Canton of Glarus.

## In a nutshell - Glarus: legal form, minimum capital and registration in the commercial register - Registration fees and notary fees variable at cantonal level - Insurance obligations: AVS, LPP and LAMal also for employers - Swiss tax system at 3 levels: federal, cantonal and municipal
## Key facts - **What**: Opening a business in the Canton of Glarus requires the choice of a legal form, registration in the trade register and compliance with federal and cantonal insurance and tax obligations. - When: Registration must be made before the start of the activity; individual companies without an obligation to register must be registered for VAT purposes if they exceed the established thresholds. - Where: Canton of Glarus; cantonal office of the trade register and competent tax authorities. - Who: Future entrepreneur or founder; cantonal trade register office; AFC/ESTV for IFD and VAT; UFAS/BSV for AVS and LPP. - Amount: Minimum capital for Sagl/GmbH established by federal law; registration fees and notary fees defined at cantonal level.
Starting a business in Switzerland is a choice that always goes through the commercial register: every company based in Swiss territory must in fact be registered with the competent cantonal office, and in some cases also with a central federal register. In the Canton of Glarus, the procedure follows the federal rules of the Code of Bonds, but the rates, forms and aspects ## Practical analysis: costs and operational choices
### Minimum capital and incorporation costs The minimum capital for joint-stock companies is set by federal law (Code of Bonds) and does not vary from canton to canton: what changes, from Glarus to Zurich, are notary fees and registration fees in the cantonal register. The latter are determined by the commercial register office of the Canton of Glarus and depend on the legal form and complexity of the deed of incorporation.
For a sole proprietorship, the upfront costs are generally lower: no minimum capital or public deed is required. For a SAGL or an SA, in addition to the federal minimum capital, notary fees, cantonal registration fees and the possible establishment of a occupational pension fund for employees must be provided for.
### Tax obligations: three levels The Swiss tax system is divided into three levels: direct federal tax (DFI), cantonal tax and municipal tax. The IFD is a progressive federal tax, administered under the rules of the AFC and collected by the cantons under federal supervision. The cantonal tax is governed by the tax law of the Canton of Glarus, with a municipal multiplier that varies from municipality to municipality. This means that two companies with the same turnover may have a different tax burden depending on their location.

### Before registration 1. **Choose the right legal form**: sole proprietorship, Sagl (GmbH), AG (SA) or another form provided by the Code of Obligations. The choice affects minimum capital, liability and accounting obligations. 2. Check the cantonal requirements: each canton may require specific authorizations for certain activities (professional regulations, licences, permits). 3. Define the registered office: the address must be in Glarus in order to be registered in the cantonal register.
### Registration in the Commercial Register 4. Prepare the founding deed: for capital companies a public deed drawn up by a notary is required. For a sole proprietorship, a registration declaration with the required data. 5. Deposit the minimum capital: with a Swiss bank, with issuance of the payment confirmation required for registration. 6. Submit the application to the Commercial Register Office of the Canton of Glarus: with articles of association, founding deed, bank confirmation and identity documents of the founders. 7. Receive the UID number: necessary to operate with federal authorities and for subsequent registrations (VAT, compensation funds, etc.).
### Subsequent obligations 8. Registration for VAT purposes (if mandatory or optional) through the competent federal portal. 9. Registration as an employer with the AVS compensation fund, unemployment insurance and SUVA or other LAINF insurer. 10. Registration with the occupational pension scheme if you hire personnel subject to the BVG/LPP. 11. Registration with the cantonal tax office for cantonal and municipal tax, and filing of the DFI/IFD according to federal deadlines.
### Deadlines and updates The threshold figures (3rd pillar 3a maximums, LPP coordination deduction, UI/AL maximum, average LAMal premiums, median salary) are indexed every year: for updated amounts it is advisable to consult official federal and cantonal sources.
### Costs to budget - Commercial Register registration fees: variable at cantonal level. - Notary fees: depending on the complexity of the founding deed. - Minimum capital: for Sagl and AG/SA, defined by federal law. - Any costs for tax and legal advice.
